speaker: Dai Le
heading: BUSINESS
text:
I second the motion of the member for Calare. I spoke last week about the good and the bad of this new world we're living in of artificial intelligence—its ability to make us work more efficiently and more productively but also its potential harm to humanity.

Let me start with what artificial intelligence gets right. It can reduce paperwork for small businesses, improve services and help people work more productively, if used well. For small-business owners in Fowler, that matters. A task that once took a day may take an hour. Paperwork that kept someone at the kitchen table late at night can be dealt with before they open the shop in the morning. I, too, want the people of Fowler to have every safe AI tool that helps them compete, grow and spend more time with their families. I'm not here to stand in the way of that.

But a tool this powerful needs rules and guardrails. We are already seeing the harm. For a community like Fowler, the risk can be even greater. More than six in 10 people in Fowler speak a language other than English at home. A scam can arrive in someone's first language sounding urgent and convincing while a legitimate warning does not reach them the same way and at the same speed. An increasing example is AI voice cloning imitating loved ones and demanding money. Once that content spreads, it is hard to pull back. And when people cannot tell what is real, trust breaks down—trust in information, trust in institutions and trust in our democracy.

That's why I support this motion and the member for Calare's bill. It is not about banning AI; it is about keeping people in control of a powerful technology. The bill requires providers of certain advanced AI systems to maintain the ability to intervene, stop a system's outputs, suspend access, restrict dangerous uses or shut the system down when necessary. This is not a one-big-red-button action. It is a graduated response—restrict a harmful capability; slow the system down; suspend access; move to a safe backup; shut it down when there is no safe alternative. That is not anti innovation; it is common sense.

For example, many of you who use today's cars would have—my car at least has it—a reversing safety sensor. So, when I'm reversing out of a car park or my driveway for instance, even though I can see an oncoming car, my car senses an oncoming car and automatically stops my car from reversing further. That way, we do not collide, or there's a prediction that we can collide. Sometimes, it's annoying to use, because I think I have my driving under control. But it has been designed to protect me and others from a mistake that I may not see coming. So we accept that safety feature because we understand the cost of getting it wrong. If we expect safety systems in cars on our driveways, surely we should expect meaningful safety systems from the companies developing the most powerful technology of our time.

There's also a physical side to the AI revolution—data centres, as the member for Calare mentioned. AI does not exist only on our screen; it needs enormous infrastructure, using electricity and water and land. Australia has around 165 operational data centres, with at least 225 more proposed or under development, and they are being fast-tracked before any legislation to safeguard them is in place. They are being built as we speak. Much of that growth is in New South Wales and Victoria. At least two data centres have been approved in Fowler, with more proposed. People deserve answers. Who pays for the electricity, the water and the infrastructure? Can the government guarantee that Fowler families will not face higher power bills? This needs to be addressed, and the member for Calare has done so in this bill.

I welcome innovation. But innovation must serve the people, not leave them behind. And this bill is a sensible step towards responsible planning, stronger safeguards and putting ethics back into infrastructure like data centres and AI development. We need to have that in place, and we have to do that—if we're taking the lead in the world with other legislation, such as the banning of social media for under-16s, surely this is more critical. This will have wider impact on our community and our society.

That is how we can make AI work for Australians. Rather than asking Australians to simply adjust to AI, we need to ensure that the Australian public can trust this new technology that's being rolled out so fast in front of us. Thank you.

speaker: Josh Burns
heading: COMMITTEES
subheading: Public Accounts and Audit Joint Committee; Report
text:
On behalf of the Joint Committee of Public Accounts and Audit, I present the following reports: Report 516: Inquiry into Commonwealth financial statements 2023-24 and 2024-25 and Report 517: Annual report 2025-26.

Report made a parliamentary paper in accordance with standing order 39(e).

by leave—First of all, I present the report of the Joint Committee of Public Accounts and Audit No. 516: Inquiry into Commonwealth financial statements 2023-24 and 2024-25.

The annual auditing of financial accounting and reporting by Commonwealth entities by the Australian National Audit Office provides assurance to the parliament on the financial position of the Australian government and the expenditure of taxpayer money.

This report considers the findings of both the 2023-24 and 2024-25 financial statements audits, with a particular focus on three areas of interest to the committee: compliance with legislation, including section 83 of the Australian Constitution; the information technology environment; and the governance of emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence.

Legislative non-compliance has increased across the two audit periods. While the committee welcomes evidence that entities have accepted the seriousness of issues identified by the ANAO, and are taking active steps toward remediation, the committee remains concerned by the number of breaches that persist across multiple audit cycles.

The IT control environment continues to account for the largest proportion of audit findings. It is clear to the committee that IT governance and controls continue to be a persistent challenge for entities.

The committee was encouraged by the approaches undertaken by the Department of Defence and NBN Co, both of which have successfully resolved findings relating to unauthorised post-separation access of IT networks. In these cases, resolution was achieved by addressing the issue as a whole-of-business issue rather than one confined to IT alone. The committee considers this approach instructive for the broader public sector and encourages other entities to apply similar methods.

The committee also considered the continued growth in the use of AI and other emerging technologies across the public sector. While the committee did not investigate the use of AI across the public sector in depth, it will continue to monitor whether governance frameworks are keeping pace with the rate of adoption and the range of emerging use cases.

One recommendation made by the committee was that the ANAO tables at least annually a report that examines public sector entities use and preparedness for emerging digital technologies.

I want to acknowledge and thank Senator Matt O'Sullivan for his service as deputy chair until March 2026 and thank the current deputy chair, the Hon. Scott Buchholz MP, for his help, commitment and support.

I thank all committee members for their contributions to this inquiry, and I commend that report to the House.

I am also pleased to present Report 517: Annual report 2025-26I've already given it to the clerks.

Under the Public Accounts and Audit Committee Act 1951, the committee is required to report annually to the parliament on the work it has undertaken.

The committee's work includes reviewing Australian National Audit Office reports and conducting inquiries where it identifies issues needing further examination. The committee determines the audit priorities of the parliament and makes recommendations to the government on the budget estimates of the Australian National Audit Office and the Parliamentary Budget Office. The committee can request a post-election review of the PBO's operations and did so following the 2025 election.

In 2025-26, the committee held 27 meetings, including seven public hearings. The committee commenced eight inquiries, tabled three reports, undertook a range of non-inquiry activities in line with legislative responsibilities and met with delegations from Kiribati and Cambodia, both highly successful. We completed inquiries in 2025-26, including into the effectiveness of Australia's National Anti-Doping Scheme and the procurement processes for supporting services for victims of child sexual abuse.

Again, I thank the deputy chair and all of the committee members, and I also want to pay a special tribute to the secretariat, who are outstanding public servants and serve the committee with distinction.

I commend the report to the House.

I ask leave of the House to present executive minutes on reports of the Joint Committee of Public Accounts and Audit, if that's possible.

Leave granted.

I present the executive minutes on reports 463, 472, 477, 479, 485, 486, 488, 491, 492, 498, 502, 504, 509, 511, 512, 514 and 515 of the Joint Committee of Public Accounts and Audit.

speaker: David Pocock
heading: BILLS
subheading: Universities Accord (Opening the Doors of Opportunity) Bill 2026; Second Reading
text:
I'd like to start by saying that I welcome the Universities Accord (Opening the Doors of Opportunity) Bill 2026 and the reforms it contains to how we fund universities, and I intend to support it. However, the very clear consensus from evidence presented to the Senate committee inquiry is that it needs amendments before it should pass the Senate.

First and foremost, while fixing how we fund universities, the bill does nothing to address student contributions and the crushing debt impacts from Job-Ready Graduates. After four years in power and having railed against Job-ready Graduates in opposition, it should be unbelievable—unfortunately, it isn't—that the Albanese government have failed to act on JRG. First they kicked it to ATEC. Now ATEC is saying there'll be no advice until next year and no change until 2028 at the earliest. In that time, students will continue to accrue $50,000-plus debts for a humanities degree, a degree that we know is more important than ever in the face of AI.

I'm moving an amendment that would seek to expedite this process. The overwhelming consensus from the Senate inquiry was that the most concerning thing about this bill is the extraordinary powers that it gives the current minister and any future minister to intervene in our universities. While some of these powers have been wound back, they remain excessive. I believe further amendment is required specifically to remove ministerial power to set course-level caps for international students, cap demand-driven places for Indigenous students and set provider-specific funding conditions. As a Senate, we should be a check on executive power and we should fight tooth and nail not to provide this level of power to any future minister. These sorts of changes should be subject to scrutiny. They should have to come through this parliament and be judged by elected representatives on behalf of the people that send them to this place.

In circumstances where this bill passes unamended, QUT highlighted the potential perils and vulnerability to politicisation of standard university operational decisions. I'll quote from their submission. It said:

The Bill would create an avenue for stakeholders dissatisfied with such decisions to seek Ministerial intervention in operational matters that should remain within established institutional governance processes.

It said the existence of these powers:

… would encourage stakeholders to seek Ministerial intervention whenever an institutional decision becomes contentious. Refusing to intervene could then become as politically consequential as intervening.

I don't understand why the minister would even want these powers. Can you imagine the lobbying that it opens them up to and the public criticism where they do or don't make a decision that may or may not be ideologically aligned with a certain group? Not only could a minister ban a specific course for ideological reasons or at the behest of a vested interest; they could also mandate that certain courses be taught. Given what we've seen overseas, it's really not hard to imagine a government banning all sorts of things, such as welcomes to country or pride events on campus, or interfering with what universities teach about climate change, genocide or the Holocaust. No government should have this sort of power to impose ideologies on our universities. As Doctor Byron succinctly put it, while the government could be worried about a future rogue Senate, the Senate should be worried about a future rogue government. That encapsulates the concerns about handing this sort of extraordinary power to the minister.

Both I and the coalition will move an amendment that would seek to remove these powers. In my second reading amendment, I talk about the need to better define equity. The University of Canberra highlighted the shortcomings with the current definition:

… the ACT is largely excluded from the Government's Needs-based Funding model, with no support for Low Socio-Economic Status (Low SES) or regional students. Proposed methodology of using Low SES does not recognise any disadvantaged University of Canberra students from the ACT. We have not received support funding in 2026 for most of our disadvantaged students and now expect to be underfunded into 2027.

The 2021 Socio-Economic Indexes for Areas (SEIFA) are not adequate in identifying disadvantage in the ACT. Using these tables there are no Low-SES areas in the ACT. This is a product of good urban planning but statistically hides disadvantaged individuals.

Canberra has pockets of extreme disadvantage, and this needs to be recognised. We have to have a system where students who need more support get it and universities who need to provide that support are provided with additional funding to do exactly that. This really rough way of calculating low-SES or regional students just doesn't cut it. We have to do better as a country in terms of collecting data and ensuring that universities like the University of Canberra aren't missing out.

The purpose of this bill is managed growth, but, as experts like Doctor Andrew Norton highlighted, 'the bill does not appropriate any new funding for additional student places'. He said:

By contrast, the bill has two new features that will reduce how many student places universities can offer.

This clearly stands in contrast to the stated aim of managed growth. Another of my amendments seeks to set a floor in the total allocation pool. A further concern is around parliamentary oversight. The two determinations that set the size of the whole system, the domestic total allocation pool and the international pool are expressly exempt from disallowance. Every decision beneath them is declared not to be a legislative instrument, including place allocations, core and growth determinations, and international allocations. We should not be allowing this as a Senate. We should have a say on these decisions of the executive. They should be up for debate. They should be up for disallowance. I urge fellow senators to ensure that we do not hand these powers to the executive in perpetuity. One of my amendments seeks to change this and give the parliament, rather than the minister of the day, oversight of these crucial matters—crucial not just for our university sector but for the future of our country.

I'd like to thank my team for the huge amount of work that they put into this bill and this inquiry. Based on the evidence provided to the Senate Committee, I requested 23 amendments to this bill, all based on what I'd heard from the university sector and from experts. Unfortunately, at the time of making these remarks, only five have been circulated, and I note the Greens are yet to circulate any amendments. For a bill this important, I think it speaks to a failure of process. As senators, we need to have the opportunity to move amendments to bills, and that requires access to drafting in a timely way that enables us to discuss with colleagues and to seek support before the bill is in the Senate like this. I'd like to thank those in the drafting office for the amazing work that they do. We know that you're under the pump.

But, as a crossbencher, again I would like to raise with the government, with the President, the lack of drafting resources for the crossbench. I can't speak of how the major parties experience it, but, as a crossbencher, it is incredibly difficult to get anything drafted in a timely manner, and I don't think that's good enough for our democracy. Elected representatives, regardless of where you're from, who you're here representing or which state or territory you're representing, should have access to drafting, where you can put forward your amendments in good faith, have conversations with colleagues, and then, when it comes down to it, they're either supported or not supported.

Finally, I'd like to thank the committee for all their work and stakeholders for their comprehensive, detailed and constructive submissions on this legislation. Too often the public does not see the genuinely good faith work that happens in this place—the collaboration and the collegiate way that Senate committees can work a lot of the time, obviously not all of the time. I think we should continue to highlight that as senators. So while I have these concerns, I thank the government for the direction they are heading in, and I commend my amendments to the Senate. I foreshadow my second reading amendments.

speaker: David Shoebridge
heading: BILLS
subheading: Universities Accord (Opening the Doors of Opportunity) Bill 2026; Second Reading
text:
I rise first of all to acknowledge the work of my colleague Senator Faruqi in this space, endorse her comments and particularly note the raft of concerns about this bill that remain unaddressed including the genuine cost-of-living crisis that we know students are facing with ever mounting HECS debt. I haven't spoken to a student who remembers getting a haircut on the HECS debt, but I've spoken to plenty of students who are looking at a lifetime of debt for simply wanting to get an education to contribute to society.

We still don't see a solution for the so-called Job-Ready Graduates scheme that saw these appalling cost hikes for arts degrees. It was a conscious attack from the coalition to dumb down our universities and to attack critical thinking. We're five years—it feels like forever—into a Labor government, and they still haven't addressed that despite repeated offers from the Greens to solve that. Degree costs have continued on their upward path. Student payments remain below the poverty line. These are the core issues in the university sector that despite the name on the box of this bill—it's called the Universities Accord (Opening the Doors of Opportunity) Bill 2026. Again, as we know, the doors of opportunity are very narrowly open under Labor, particularly for students who don't have family support, those who are first generation at university, those who are considering career that isn't in the finance sector or a highly paying sector but is essential for our society like teaching, nursing, social work, critical thinking. They're the ones who continue to be under the gun despite five years of a Labor government.

There's one other thing that I think absolutely needs to be addressed with urgency in the university sector, and it's playing out in university campuses in my home state of New South Wales. It's playing out on the campuses of the University of New South Wales, of the University of Sydney, of UTS, of Macquarie University, but I know it's playing out across universities Australia wide. While there's talk of building opportunities—what this bill talks about—what students and academics are facing right now are universities reaching for AI to dumb down degrees, to replace staff and to put at risk the reputations of some of our finest institutions. Last week, the University of New South Wales said it had signed this so-called strategic partnership with OpenAI—a US owned, tech-bro owned vampire company who has no interest in building Australia's education sector, who has no interest in educating Australians and who definitely has no interest in our universities being competitive. Without putting any guardrails in, without talking to the staff and without articulating what the strategic partnership will mean for job security, for the quality of degrees, for teaching, they make this big announcement. This is the statement that UNSW made:

The collaboration, one of the largest AI education deployments in the Asia-Pacific region, aims to help ensure graduates are equipped to use AI critically, ethically and effectively.

Who are they partnering with? OpenAI, the same US tech-bro owned corporation that let its agents escape the sandbox and run wild.

What are the what are the checks and balances being proposed here? Where are the restraints in how our university sector rolls out AI to endanger our research capability? It's not all upside with AI. There's serious risk of deskilling our researchers, rogue AI agents taking that research and heading off heaven knows where. There's complete silence from this government about—not a whisper about one of our premier universities and, at different times, one of our highest ranked university on global ratings uncritically rolling out a foreign multinational AI player right throughout its universities in what it describes as 'the largest AI education deployment in the Asia-Pacific'.

That's not a good news story. That's a flashing-lights warning story. It's not just that. Less than a week after that, the University of Sydney made an announcement as well. The University of Sydney comes out and talks about 'a university-wide investment in AI to ensure every student and staff member has free and equitable access to advanced AI tools'. And then we get this guff:

Tomorrow's leaders will also need to understand AI's ethical, social and environmental impacts, and possess the ability to work with this technology critically and responsibly. We will support you for that future by providing equitable access to advanced AI tools.

Whatever the University of Sydney's Vice President of Operations, Ms Gower, might say about it being a human centred approach to AI, ask the staff—the academics, the people who are going to have to deliver for this. How they see this deal of the University of Sydney with the same bunch of US tech-bro AI vampires is as a threat. Because, at the same time that the university went out and made its announcement that they're going to be incorporating a foreign owned AI into every aspect of the university's operations, the NTEU members, the people who actually have to teach, do the research and undertake the critical thinking at University of Sydney, were out on strike seeking enforceable consultation protections around AI. This is how this is how managerial and out of touch management at our universities is—these vice-chancellors and their cronies that hang around them, paid a million bucks a year and more. I think, in Sydney, they also get a free, posh residence. You get a million bucks in your bank account and a free, posh residence if you're the vice-chancellor in Sydney, and then you use that privilege to roll out AI and take away the jobs of the actual teaching staff.

And we get Labor coming in here with their—what is it named?—Universities Accord (Opening the Doors of Opportunity) Bill. Well, under Labor, the door's been opened to vampire, US owned AI to come and march through our universities and take away jobs, destroy the critical thinking that we're going to need for our students and continue to empower the managerial class to run through our universities.

I want to say, on behalf of my party, the Greens, that we stand in solidarity with the NTEU members who are on strike, asking for genuine, enforceable consultation protections before universities like Sydney or UNSW enter into these multiyear deals. And we want to make sure that they're enforceable rights so that the vice-chancellors on their million bucks a year and their $500,000, $700,000, $800,000 per annum human-development staff-squashing managerial teams don't get to destroy our universities. The only door of opportunity that seems to be opening here is the door of opportunity for US big tech to come in, deskill and put at enormous risk some of our most important institutions.

I would urge the government to go and look at what the community thinks about this and the lack of action on protecting our universities from the rollout of US owned AI, because you have a look at the comments on social media about Sydney university's post and they're not saying: 'Oh, amazing—wonderful opportunity. I'm glad you've invited these robber barons in to come and attack our university.' They're calling it 'despicable garbage'. They're calling it 'fascism-maxxing'. They're naming it for what it is.

There's some marginal good in this bill. The marginal good is great. But there's this massive risk, and it's not academic; it happened last week—the week before this bill got rolled in to literally destroy the integrity, the reputation, the qualities of our universities, because, under Labor, US big tech, US AI companies, are marching through our universities, and the staff are on the front lines fighting it, going into industrial action, saying, 'You can't do this without us.'

What's the answer from Labor? Nothing, because it turns out that the same big tech companies that are talking to the vice-chancellor at Sydney university and schmoozing with the vice-chancellor at UNSW are in there with a ready-access door to the Prime Minister, trying to do a job on creatives and trying to get a red carpet to roll out their AI vision right across this country—to steal our water, our power and our data and, in this case, to have that march through some of our most important institutions.

Unless this government is willing to come and work with the Greens to address the risk of AI through our universities—you can pass as many 'opening the doors of opportunity' bills as you like, but, unless we address the risk of foreign owned AI through the march of our institutions, this won't amount to a hill of beans.

speaker: Vanessa Bleyer
heading: STATEMENTS BY SENATORS
text:
Off the far north-west coast of Tasmania is an island, Robbins Island. Its traditional Palawa name is Pilitika. It is rich in Aboriginal cultural heritage and of profound significance to the Palawa Pakana people. It contains landforms of global geological and geomorphological significance. Its complex coastal systems serve as an international index site for studying past climate changes and sea-level histories. It is on the migratory pathway of the critically endangered orange-bellied parrot, which doesn't just instinctively fly over but stops and forages on the island. It is home to the last remaining disease-free population of the endangered Tasmanian devil in the world. Elsewhere in Tasmania, a facial tumour disease is decimating Tasmanian devil populations.

Now, wait for this, and I hope you're all sitting down: last year, in 2025, this Labor government approved a wind farm at Pilitika/Robbins Island. Construction of turbines will destroy sites of Aboriginal cultural heritage, destroy sites of global geological significance and cause the extinction of the orange-bellied parrot as the turbine blades pulverise the last parrots that survive. Construction of a bridge from mainland Tasmania to Pilitika/Robbins Island will introduce diseased Tasmanian devils and decimate the last healthy wild population. Construction of a wharf will deprive us forever of studying sea-level histories at a time of climate crisis, when we need it most. Like every development, there's a right place and a wrong place. This is simply the wrong place for a wind farm.

You'll be pleased to know I'm the bearer of good news. Something has just happened which means that this government should now bring the proposed wind farm at Pilitika/Robbins Island to an end. It was a condition of this government's approval of the Robbins Island wind farm that, within six months of the date of approval, the proponent of the wind farm—backed by a megarich Philippines based company, by the way—must submit an orange-bellied parrot survey plan to this government for approval. The proponent did not. It was a condition of this government's approval that the proponent notify this government within two business days of failing to comply with the condition. The proponent did not. The big foreign corporation behind the proposed wind farm obviously cares not for the laws of this nation, just like it obviously cares not for the irreplaceable natural and cultural wonders of Pilitika-Robbins Island.

On the other hand, we hear this government talking so much about how it upholds the rule of law and that the rule of law is a foundational principle of Australia's democracy. It follows that it must care very much for the laws of this nation. So, no doubt, this government is going to do what the law says that it should because of the breached conditions and immediately revoke the approval of the wind farm at Pilitika-Robbins Island. No doubt, this government is going to do what the law says it should and prosecute the proponent for its serious statutory offence in breaching the conditions. Surely this government is not more concerned about appeasing a big corporation and making decisions for that big corporation instead of for us. I and so many whom I represent in Tasmania eagerly await the news from this Labor government that it will adhere to the rule of law and that this monstrosity of a wind farm—100 turbines, each over 200 metres high, and in absolutely the wrong place—is over.

Speaking of developments that are absolutely in the wrong place, I note a proposed data centre in the Tamar Valley in northern Tasmania that remains controversial. Recently, a local council in Tasmania approved that AI data centre at what was previously the site for Gunns proposed pulp mill. Let me tell you, that place and I go way back. When I was a lawyer, we ran more court cases to stop that proposed dirty, stinking pulp mill than to stop any other proposed development in this nation. We challenged every single state and federal government approval. This was because that site in the Tamar Valley is not the place for a pulp mill. The noise that the pulp mill would have generated and the light that the pulp mill would have emitted would have been grossly disruptive to the residents of the Tamar Valley, and it would have permanently damaged the then $50-million-a-year tourism industry. The massive amounts of water that the pulp mill would have needed could not have been delivered, because the presence of threatened flora species where the pipeline was intended to be built would have prohibited it. For all these reasons, the pulp mill failed.

For the same reasons, a noisy, light-emitting and water intensive AI data centre at the same site as the proposed Gunns pulp mill cannot proceed, in what is now a $100-million-a-year tourism industry. It might have local council approval, but I can't see how it could get federal government approval under our national environment laws. Big business and the Tasmanian government sought to ram through the pulp mill, but, as a community, we stood up and saw it off. As a community, we can and we will do the same for this AI data centre.

We know that data centres are deeply unpopular across the whole of Australia, particularly in Tasmania. A petition tabled this month by my Greens colleagues in Tasmania's state parliament opposing the development of AI data centres was one of the largest in the state's history. Tasmanians called for an immediate moratorium on non-complete artificial intelligence and data facilities until strict protective guardrails are put in place.

We need a moratorium on AI data centre developments across the whole nation now. That is the Greens position and that is the public's expectation of all of us in this place. We can't wait until next year, when this government says it's going to introduce proposed laws, because, in the meantime, companies like Firmus are going to ram their proposals through local planning processes. Local councils aren't even equipped to deal with that. AI data centres were not even a sparkle in anyone's eye when the planning schemes were prepared. The only people that benefit from these developments are the big tech corporations.

The company that is seeking to build the data centre in Tasmania's Tamar Valley, Firmus, is run by a convicted fraudster. Can we really take him at his word? We can't, and I'll give you some evidence as to why. Firmus has just appealed the local council decision to approve the data centre at the proposed Gunns pulp mill site in an effort to allow it to run diesel powered generators at the site. It had promised that its data centres would be powered by renewable energy.

These big tech corporations are misleading our communities. They are misleading our governments, and they are proposing developments that are in the wrong place. The community won the fight against Gunns proposed pulp mill and the community will win this fight against this proposed AI data centre.

speaker: Kate Chaney
heading: MATTERS OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
text:
The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This statement was posted on X last week by Jacob Coxon, a researcher who had just resigned from Anthropic and had previously worked at OpenAI. In the weeks since, the statement has been validated by the leading voices of the AI industry—Dario Amodei, Sam Altman, Elon Musk, Demis Hassabis and others. These industry leaders have all publicly come forward to make the same point: AI is moving too fast and its risks are becoming too great. Dario Amodei wrote that he believed AI could take over the entire internet in the next six to 12 months. Elon Musk wrote that AI is potentially more dangerous than nukes.

Now, we've known about the risks of AI for a long time. AI tools can supercharge cyberwarfare. They can help terrorist groups build biological weapons. They can allow foreign regimes to undertake large-scale disinformation campaigns during elections in our country. And they could escape human control, which we've seen a number of times in previous months. But when we have all the CEOs of the leading AI companies reaching a rare consensus—that AI is moving too fast to control—it is time for us to pause and think: What can we do from Australia? How can we prepare ourselves for the risks? And who is protecting the interests of Australia and Australians? Ultimately, most of these sci-fi-sounding risks may not come true, but we should absolutely be preparing for them just in case.

Instead of more doom and gloom, I want to offer solutions. The first one is the simplest and the most significant. The Albanese government must increase its funding of the Australian AI Safety Institute. The AI Safety Institute, or AISI for short, is our frontline defence against frontier AI models developed overseas. Its responsibility is to test new AI models and agents for risks, work with our government to develop appropriate responses and collaborate with international AI safety institutes. But the AISI is drastically underfunded. It receives less than $8 million a year, and with that funding it's expected to identify if the latest AI model produced by Anthropic could be used to hack our banks. It's expected to identify if the latest OpenAI agent can escape human control and start replicating; to identify if the latest Google model could help a disgruntled, angry lone wolf to build a biological weapon to be released in a school or a synagogue or a festival; and to prepare Australia for risks that could do billions of dollars of damage and cause untold suffering to countless Australians.

I'm calling on the government to increase AISI funding to $100 million a year. Now, this is a rounding error against a federal budget of over $700 billion. It's a rounding error against the damages and harm that it could prevent. It's also a rounding error compared to the productivity benefits that we're relying on AI to deliver that depend on safe uptake. There are very few line items in the budget with such a strong business case. Everyone I've talked to across the AI industry—across business, civil society, experts and community—agrees that the AISI needs more funding to keep up with the incredible pace of AI development. The UK's equivalent institute gets 16 times more funding, and as a result it's widely recognised as the international gold standard for AI safety. The UK doesn't have its own frontier model, but it's a leader in AI safety anyway. This simply must be funded properly. None of us believe that the tech billionaires, Donald Trump or Xi Jinping will ensure that these technologies are safe for us.

Beyond more resources, there's so much else that we could be doing. Firstly is access. The AI Safety Institute should be given the power to compel AI developers to provide early access to their models before they're deployed in Australia. Currently, frontier AI developers, like Anthropic and OpenAI, often do provide early access to safety institutes, but this is done on an entirely voluntary basis. What if Anthropic chooses in the future not to provide early access to a revolutionary cyberwarfare tool like Mythos? What if Chinese models start entering Australia en masse without our AI Safety Institute testing them first?

Secondly—disclosure. Frontier AI developers should be required to provide essential information to AISI and the Australian government. This means sharing a safety framework describing how the AI developers identify and test for risks. It means mandatory critical incident reports when a serious safety risk emerges after deployment.

Earlier this year, OpenAI and Anthropic revealed that a number of their AI models had escaped control and escaped their testing environment. Australians only know about that because of media investigations and because the companies chose to tell us. This has to change. Australia needs clarity about the true risks and capabilities of these models.

Thirdly—crisis management. Australia's crisis management framework should be updated to include AI crises both as standalone incidents and as amplifiers of existing hazards like pandemics or natural disasters. Before COVID-19 arrived, Australia had a detailed pandemic plan ready to go, and it meant our early response was among the best in the OECD. We have no equivalent plan for an AI enabled cyberattack on the electricity grid or an AI system deployed in government producing catastrophic outputs. Those risks could unfold within hours, faster than the time it would take to convene a meeting to discuss a response if no plan existed.

Our Security of Critical Infrastructure Act needs the same update. It doesn't currently clearly capture data centres hosting AI models and it does nothing to ensure the operators of our energy, water and health infrastructure are actually preparing for AI enabled cyberattacks.

Fourthly—cooperation. Australia should be working with countries like Canada, Japan, South Korea, the UK and our partners across the European Union, nations that share our interest in AI being developed safely but individually lack the leverage to set the terms on their own. Together, these middle powers represent a substantial share of the world's AI-using population and a large market for the companies that build these models. A coordinated position among us—on minimum safety expectations, on transparency requirements, on incident reporting, on what a frontier developer must disclose before releasing a new model—carries far more weight than any one of us could achieve alone.

The International Network of AI Safety Institutes gives us the start of this architecture. We should be using it and using it quickly. This is not a naive call for a single global treaty that will never happen. It's a practical case for coalition building among the countries that have the most to lose from a race to the bottom and the most to gain from getting this right. Only by working with fellow middle powers to develop consistent rules can we ensure that our AI future is one in which we're excited to live.

Lastly—data centres. In the meantime, unlocking the ability for data centres to be built in a manner that's sustainable and beneficial for Australians will also build leverage and sovereignty over this industry. The longer-term economic benefits of data centres may remain ambiguous but the strategic and geopolitical advantages are significant. The government must quickly develop appropriate copyright protections so that creatives have meaningful control over their work and AI developers are able to train and build data centres in Australia if they appropriately compensate those creators.

The government must also develop its binding AI standards to ensure that data centres: are powered by 100 per cent additional renewable energy; are highly water efficient; clearly benefit the Australian community; and are transparent with the data being used. Once these guardrails are in place, data centre development can become a significant asset to Australia and Australians.

There are many people I talk to who ask why we're building this new technology at all. The truth is that the promise of AI is enormous—supercharged medical research, rising living standards, improved accessibility. But the promise and the peril of AI are not separate stories. They're the same story, told from two different vantage points. A model capable enough to accelerate a cancer diagnosis is a model capable enough to help someone build a weapon. A system trusted enough to run our aged-care packages is a system dangerous enough to repeat the mistakes of robodebt at a far greater scale. We cannot choose to embrace one side of this technology while wishing away the other. They arrive together or not at all.

That's why this cannot be treated as a distant hypothetical debate for some future parliament to resolve. The decisions being made in the boardrooms of San Francisco and Beijing this year will shape the world Australian kids will inherit. Waiting for certainty before we act is not caution; it's abdication. We do not have the luxury of waiting for the risks to fully materialise before we respond to them, because by then it will be too late to respond at all. But the only way we can realise the promise of AI is if the government acts urgently to deal with its peril.

speaker: Basem Abdo
heading: MATTERS OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
text:
I thank the member for Curtin for bringing this matter of public importance here today. AI is essential policy conversation across the world that demands our full attention. When it comes to AI, we as a government are driven by progress and principles. We agree that this emerging technology represents a generational opportunity for Australia if properly harnessed. It presents immense opportunities just as it carries significant risks, and our focus on progress and principles means that our approach as a government is to engage with both simultaneously with seriousness and urgency. It is relevant to our economy, workforce, national security and online safety as well as research, science, innovation and the productivity of our economy.

When it comes to action, this government is taking world-leading action guided by a clear set of principles. The Albanese government's National AI Plan sets out three key pillars which are focused on capturing the opportunity before us, sharing in its benefits and keeping Australians safe. As announced by the Prime Minister, the government will introduce AI laws in Australia's interests—a nationally consistent regulatory framework that will work with the states and territories to set minimum requirements for large data centres. This world-leading framework will ensure Australia can capture the opportunity, share the benefits and keep Australians safe.

Over the past nine months alone, the government has released the National AI Plan; released national expectations for data centres and AI infrastructure; established the AI Safety Institute; announced that Australia will legislate AI safety and a world-leading artificial intelligence framework to ensure that the development of AI in Australia is aligned with our interests; established the Office of AI in the Prime Minister's department to deliver the development of the standards; and established a 'buy Australian' initiative for Australian-made AI. The Prime Minister will be at the UN General Assembly next week, where a key focus of his will be technology regulation. The Deputy Prime Minister and Assistant Minister Charlton also recently travelled to the United States to engage on Australia's national AI standards and issues to do with AI safety. It's an all-hands-on-deck effort, engaging every part of the government.

I have previously spoken about a proposed large-scale data centre in Campbellfield, on the site of the old Ford plant, in my electorate. I have stressed the need for communities like mine to understand what impact this development may have on our local area, including the potential impact on local energy and water resources and ongoing noise, as well as whether this is the best use of what was a key manufacturing hub for our community. I was devastated when the Liberals drove Ford and local jobs on that site out of our area, and that site means a lot to me and to our community. We all remember the workers who were there, who made things in Australia and who, in doing so, helped make Australia. When it comes to AI, it should be done the Australian way—without undercutting conditions or dividing communities or damaging our environment. Major industrial developments need to contribute to local jobs and local opportunities and must take into account our local environment and the future of our region.

As AI demand and reliance on cloud computing grow, data centre investment in our area must happen in ways that deliver positive outcomes for our community. While planning decisions and approvals are not a matter for federal government, I have made it clear that the Albanese Labor government has set out clear expectations for data centres and AI infrastructure to ensure that investments provide tangible benefits, both locally and across Australia. Operators must prioritise Australia's national interests not only by strengthening our security and resilience but also by delivering benefits for our local communities. Any proposal will be required to bring additional renewable energy to power their site, and we're acting to make sure they don't put upward pressure on energy prices with our world-leading rules.

They will also be expected to manage water responsibly, create well paid local jobs and skills, and back startups and research innovation and supply chains. Data centre developments must meet these expectations. Our community deserves clear answers, genuine consultation and transparent planning processes aligned with the federal government's clear expectations for data centres and AI infrastructure. I will continue to advocate strongly for our area and for the long-term liveability, sustainability and wellbeing of our growing community, just as the Albanese government is fully engaged on the opportunities and risks presented by AI.

speaker: Claire Clutterham
heading: ADJOURNMENT
text:
Artificial intelligence and efficient and effective regulation can coexist. Government and industry can collaborate with respect to AI for the benefit of the Australian people. The private sector and public sector can realise a shared vision and goals when it comes to artificial intelligence. But all of this takes leadership underpinned by three critical things: decisiveness, targeted stakeholder consultation and expertise.

That is the approach this government is taking with respect to AI. By bringing government and industry together to develop policy solutions, it's possible to harness the opportunities, reduce the known risks and plan for future ones. Partnerships of this nature mean there's no need to choose between letting innovation grow and flourish without controls or regulating to paralyse development. Regulation or innovation is a false choice. Both are important, with regulation needing to safely facilitate innovation, creativity, competition and entrepreneurship, not paralyse them.

Another false choice is deciding now whether AI will be an existential threat to the human race and then regulating on the basis of that choice. This is lazy, populist, apocalyptic thinking that helps no-one, creates unnecessary fear and discourages populations from embracing opportunity. It also paints industry as the bad guys when, in actual fact, it is industry that has the technology we want and that the Australian people expect we will have.

Most reasonable Australians will also accept that accessing and using artificial intelligence does require a level of regulation. It does not mean more government or bigger government for the sake of it. It means targeted government action informed by public sector and private sector industrial expertise, so that relevant issues like urban and regional planning, energy and water use, economic development, workforce planning, education, service delivery, organisational accountability and community confidence can be confidently and expertly managed. This is to make sure that once a particular aspect of artificial intelligence really gets going, we have the understanding and means to intervene—not to paralyse it but to manage it in the event that unintended consequences begin to play out.

First and foremost, regulation with respect to artificial intelligence must have two key objectives. Regulation must both reduce harm and promote timely access to evidence based technological resources that benefit people. Achieving these two objectives requires consideration of different criteria.

Firstly, regulation must be proportionately incremental, integrating lessons learned from measurable data at each step along the technology's development. It must also recognise and reflect that there are different regulatory layers and address them in a tailored way. Regulating the AI infrastructure layer, the AI frontier layer and then the AI application layer will require different approaches, and some layers may require less regulation than others.

Regulation must also reflect and speak to existing public policy frameworks such as competition, industrial relations and energy. And, in this sense, it must be developed in a way which does not impose disproportionate or new and excessive compliance and reporting burdens on industry. It must be developed in a way that is proportionate to the actual risk and the actual evidence based opportunity. It should be designed in the way that the technology should be—with gateways, so a single regulatory action does not lead to an irreversible outcome or cause unnecessary paralysis. Finally, regulation must encourage trust and confidence between government and industry because it's only through effective and efficient partnerships between government and industry that we will be able to build the foundations upon which the benefits can be safely harnessed and the risks minimised.

We are already seeing a divergence of regulatory approaches across the globe. The EU is proceeding by prioritising rights based safeguards, the US is prioritising innovation and China is prioritising strategic control. But global collaboration is crucial. International interoperability is crucial to ensure that regulation is not only compatible but fair, allowing all nations the opportunity to harness the benefits of artificial intelligence. That is the challenge before us and that is what the Prime Minister was calling for in Australia's national statement at the UN last month. That call was urgent and that call was right.

speaker: Anthony Norman Albanese
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE
text:
I thank the member for Barton for her question. Indeed, AI offers extraordinary opportunities for Australia, for our growth, for investment, for productivity and for businesses such as those I'll speak with tonight at the Australian Industry Group about using AI to benefit their productivity and therefore to be able to grow. Our government knows that, and that's why we're legislating Australian standards for AI. That's why we're also consulting across the board, engaging seriously with other nations as well as with AI companies themselves, so we can make sure that AI stands for Australia's interests, harnessing its power as a tool to help us build a stronger economy.

We know that we need humanity to shape AI rather than the other way around. That is why we've established the AI committee that has been stood-up in a bipartisan fashion and has already begun its work under the leadership of the member for Maribyrnong and Senator Duniam in the other place. The hack by a frontier AI agent into government websites brought home to Australians that some of the risks which are there are very real indeed. We took strong action on that and made our nation's view clear that the breach was completely unacceptable.

It is clear for everyone to see that the AI genie is well and truly out of the bottle. We can't pretend that it doesn't exist and isn't already having an impact on the way that we work, the way that we engage and, indeed, the way that politics is conducted as well. That is why what really matters is how we respond to it and how we intervene and shape it. That is also why we are engaging with domestic and global companies and with other nations as well. We did that at the United Nations General Assembly last month. We did that as well in the meetings that we have continued to hold with major companies. We're going to make sure that Australia can gain from the benefits that can come from AI whilst mitigating the risks. That is the way forward, that is what is in Australia's national interest, and that is what we will continue to do. I encourage every member of this House to engage with this process because this will be one of the dominant issues over the next decade and beyond.

speaker: Anne Ruston
heading: BILLS
subheading: Aged Care Legislation Amendment (Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Aged Care Commissioner and Other Measures) Bill 2026; Second Reading
text:
I rise to speak to the Aged Care Legislation Amendment (Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Aged Care Commissioner and Other Measures) Bill 2026. We acknowledge that this bill establishes a permanent Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander aged-care commissioner and the bill also makes a long list of repairs to Labor's new Aged Care Act. And since the bill's introduction, it has been amended to establish a new escalation pathway for decisions regarding Labor's algorithm, which it so often gets wrong. Disappointingly, this amendment that's been put forward does not fix the flawed tool itself. Together, this bill tells you a great deal about the state of aged care in this country.

First—the commissioner. This bill gives effect to a key recommendation of the Royal Commission into Aged Care Quality and Safety, a royal commission established by the coalition. The royal commission said that this role should be in place by 1 July 2023. However, it's taken this government four years to even bring this particular issue to the parliament, so it's important that the government is held to account on making sure that it meets the commitments that it makes. A new title on the door by itself does not shorten a single wait.

Second—the repairs. Much of this bill is machinery. A large part of it writes into law interim arrangements the government had already put into place using Henry VIII powers. Those are the powers that let a minister change the effect of an act by regulation without coming back to the parliament. The government leaned on them just to keep its new system running. Those powers are due to sunset this month, so the government is here, asking the parliament to make its emergency arrangements permanent before the clock runs out.

On top of that, there are 13 technical amendments—contributions, means assessments, refundable deposits, payment methods, reviews and overpayments. Some are welcome. Clearer obligations on providers to refund fees that were overcharged and stronger powers for the regulator to deal with unreasonable prices are sensible protections for older Australians, and we absolutely support them. But this is a clean-up, not a cure. In three weeks, Labor's new Aged Care Act turns one. It is a reform this government promised would make aged care simpler, fairer and more responsive, and, within months, ministers needed emergency powers just to keep the act working. This is not the mark of a system that was ready when it first began; it's the mark of reform that was rushed.

That brings me to the third and most revealing part of the bill. For months, the government told this Senate, assessors and older Australians that a trained human was involved in every step of the assessment process. That was not true. Documents released under freedom of information show the department's own staff regarded human override as a settled position, and then it was removed from the top down, with officials learning of it three days before the tool went live. Now, nearly a year later, the government has added schedule 4 to this bill, an escalation pathway for what it calls exceptional cases. Let me be clear about what this pathway actually is. An assessor who knows the algorithm has got it wrong cannot fix it. They must get the older person's consent within seven days and they must refer the case to the department of health and aged care in Canberra, and the criteria for who even qualifies will be set out in the rules the government has not actually yet written. Schedule 4 does not put a human back in charge; it gives the computer a supervisor in Canberra.

The Senate has already passed the fix for this problem. On 2 July, this chamber passed the coalition's Aged Care Amendment (Restoring Human Override for Aged Care Needs Assessments) Bill 2026 with the support of the Australian Greens and the crossbench. It would let a qualified assessor override the algorithm on the spot, require decisions to explain how the tool was used and give every older Australian assessed since it began the right to a reassessment. In the other place, Labor used its numbers to vote down urgent consideration of it—that is, they wouldn't even let this urgent issue be debated. They simply said no and refused any further conversation. The government should remember the words of one of its own senior ministers:

… in every case there needs to be human oversight of any use of AI. We don't just hand over decision-making to abstract computer programs …

Those were the words of Minister Plibersek in the House of Representatives on 27 May. Labor set the standard. Labor did not meet it in aged care.

When the committee examined the bill, the sector told us it had lost confidence in the tool because it produced strange outcomes that were causing harm. Advocates told us the existing reconsideration process can take more than 90 days, and still the department would not accept the tool is flawed. No algorithm has ever grown old, and no older Australians should be reduced to a score generated by a computer.

While this bill tidies up some paperwork, it does nothing for older Australians who are waiting and waiting and waiting. According to the department's last report, last financial year, more than 325,000 older Australians spent time in the home-care queue. In Labor's first full year in office, it was 199,000. And last financial year, 6,436 of them died while they were waiting for care. That's more than 17 people every single day dying while waiting in a queue for aged care. That's up 93 per cent on Labor's first full year in office. Think about that. It's someone's mother or someone's husband, someone who has already been told that they need care, and this government only handed over those figures after failing to comply with two orders of this Senate.

For those who do get a package, providers tell us that many are placed on a minimum-service offering—a convenient way of just saying that they haven't been given their full package. Just 60 per cent of the funding is allocated of the assessed need. Sixty per cent of the funding is allocated to just about everyone who receives a part package for the first time. And the department has admitted it changed how it counts the waitlist so that someone on a part package no longer counts as waiting. Prior to 1 November 2025, those people remained counted on the waitlist until they received their full package. When you can't shorten a queue, the Labor Party's answer is: you refine it and you redefine it.

On home support, the government has finally retained the Commonwealth Home Support Program until at least 2029, after providers, advocates and a Senate inquiry told them. I suppose it's better late than never. On residential care, the sector needs around 10,500 new beds a year to keep pace with demand. In 2024-25, just 802 new beds were built. That is why more than 3,000 older Australians are stuck in public hospital beds with nowhere to go, and the government's answer is an increase of just 2.55 per cent, against a 4.75 per cent wage increase providers are already paying. The former Inspector-General of Aged Care put it plainly: 'The way this government is implementing aged-care reform is causing harm.'

Let's be plain about what this bill does not do. It does not restore human judgement to assessments. It does not clear the waitlist. It does not fund a single new aged-care bed. And it does not get one older Australian out of a hospital bed and into a place to receive the care they need. Behind every assessment, every review and every funding decision in this bill is an older Australian—someone who's worked, raised a family and built this country, someone now waiting for a package, an assessment, a bed or an answer. The coalition believes the person must come before the process. That means restoring human judgement to assessments. It means telling older Australians the truth about how long they will wait. And it means judging this government not by how tidy its legislation looks but by whether an older Australian can get the care that they need when they need it.

We welcome this bill, as it fixes so many problems that this government was warned of on the passage of the Aged Care Bill in the first instance, but Labor has got a very, very long way to go, because older Australians deserve better from this government. It's time this government backed in its promise of putting the care back into aged care instead of putting the 'wait' into 'waitlists'.

speaker: Anika Wells
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE
text:
I thank the member for Bean for his question and for the opportunity to join him at St Mary MacKillop College Canberra to talk to students about their own experiences online. Social media can have a devastating impact on people with eating disorders and body image issues. Toxic and predatory algorithms expose Australians to fitspiration and thinspiration content, blasting images and advice that reinforce unrealistic ideals and harmful behaviour. That is why, building on Australia's social media minimum age law, our proposed digital duty of care calls out material and conduct that encourages, promotes or instructs disordered eating as being harmful to under-18s. Social media platforms, online games and AI chatbots will be required to have systems in place to prevent young people from being exposed to pro-eating-disorder content.

To make sure companies are following their duty, the eSafety Commissioner and accredited Australian researchers need the ability to check the homework of these platforms—Australian researchers like Dr Rys Farthing of Reset.Tech and Dr Hannah Jarman of Deakin University. Dr Farthing and Dr Jarman conducted a study of 1,204 pieces of pro-eating-disorder content on social media. They created under-18 and over-18 sock-puppet accounts and reported the 1,204 pieces of content on Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, X, YouTube and Pinterest to see whether the platforms took them down. What they found was shocking but, unfortunately, unsurprising. On Instagram, only 10.7 per cent of that material was taken down. When reported to YouTube, only seven per cent of the pro-eating-disorder content was taken down. On X, it was 4.5 per cent. This is the kind of mystery-shopping-style test that social media platforms, online games and AI chatbots should be accountable for in Australia. But these Australian researchers had to conduct their study in Italy, in Poland and in Germany, because, right now, in Australia, they have no protection from legal threats.

That is the kind of transparency and accountability that the coalition want to block when they say sock puppets are an Orwellian spy operation. The coalition have asked for an explanation of why sock-puppet accounts are needed. This is why: to hold these companies to account for the harm they are causing young Australians, to not just listen to what the companies are saying but to check what they are actually doing. This is what the digital duty of care will deliver and why the coalition needs to put politics to the side and work with the parliament to get this done. (Time expired)

speaker: Fatima Payman
heading: DOCUMENTS
subheading: Cybersafety Legislation; Order for the Production of Documents
text:
I move:

That the Senate take note of the explanation.

When you make a mistake, you should own up to it. In August, officials from the Department of Infrastructure, Transport, Regional Development, Communications, Sport and the Arts told the Senate Environment and Communications Legislation Committee that certain broken links in the Ageassurance technology trial report were not broken at the time the report was handed over. This evidence, the department said, was based on evidence from the company behind the report, the UK-based Age Check Certification Scheme. It was later revealed that ACCS had lied to the Guardian Australia and Australian age-check provider KJR by claiming that AI had not been used in the preparation of the report when, in fact, it had. When asked whether the department had verified that the links had only become broken after the report was presented, an official grumbled, 'It's very difficult to go back and check what may have been replaced a year ago.'

Now, I'm not normally one to put on the tinfoil hijab, but there was something off about all this. So I took on this 'difficult task' and investigated the department's claim. Using a digital library of archived webpages, I was able to confirm that these links pointed to the wrong papers when they were supposedly accessed and when the report was handed to government. Dr Reuben Kirkham, a former computer science academic, told the committee that the existence of this archival evidence 'puts the position beyond any real doubt'.

I noted in a dissenting report that, on evidence I had seen, ACCS had misled the department and that, based on this misleading advice, the department had misled the committee. I do not believe that the department set out to mislead the committee, but I did describe the failure of the department to verify ACCS's claim as a serious dereliction of duty and recommended that the department review the incident to determine whether a breach of the APS Code of Conduct had occurred. Not only was I able to disprove the department's claim but I was able to do it so very easily. Aren't these guys supposed to be the experts? I understand that these are very serious allegations, and I do not make them lightly.

In response, the secretary of the department wrote to the chair of the committee about this issue. The secretary wrote:

I do not accept the conclusion that officials are failing in their duties if they give evidence to a committee based on advice provided to them that, at face value, can be accepted as accurate.

The representations made by officials were based on information available to them at the time and were honestly and reasonably held.

There was not one word contesting what I had said, but nor was there one word taking accountability for providing misleading evidence to a committee of the Senate. There was no acknowledgement that these officials had provided false evidence based on advice from ACCS, who have lied to multiple parties, including the government, about this report. It doesn't seem like ACCS will be penalised for this, which sends an unacceptable message: you can win contracts paid by the taxpayer, deliver shoddy work, lie to the government about it and get away with it. There won't even be a departmental investigation. It just isn't good enough. It's inevitable that the department's evidence will be revealed to be, without a doubt, incorrect. Despite this, the department has yet to acknowledge its misleading evidence, let alone apologise to the committee. Even the liars at ACCS have come out and apologised for what they now describe as 'outdated or incorrect links'. This saga of obfuscation will be for nothing.

When I brought to the attention of the Commonwealth Grants Commission that it appeared to have provided misleading evidence to the Economics Legislation Committee during estimates, it was quick to not only clarify what its evidence should have been but apologise for the error. This is the gold standard for APS accountability. Meanwhile, the department has provided incomplete responses to questions on notice and dragged out FOI timelines. It has failed to take accountability for the mistakes it has made. Years from now, these actions will make for an unseemly tale of resistance to scrutiny.

speaker: Ian Sollom
heading: Attorney General’s Office
text: Fraud is growing, and artificial intelligence is making it easier for it to be committed at scale. While cases can be complex, all too often victims tell me that they feel abandoned by the system. The CPS strategy folds fraud into organised crime and national security issues, and none of its seven priorities is actually about victims; in that regard, it differs from the previous economic crime strategy. How will the Solicitor General ensure that fraud victims are not lost in the CPS’s new approach?

speaker: Perran Moon
subheading: Royal Mail: Performance — [Emma Lewell in the Chair]
text:
Meur ras, Ms Lewell. It is an honour to serve under your chairship. I thank the hon. Member for Lagan Valley (Sorcha Eastwood) for securing this debate and for her excellent speech.

The performance of Royal Mail in Camborne, Redruth and Hayle, in the south-west of Cornwall, has been simply woeful. Constituents regularly tell me that they have gone weeks without post and, like other hon. Members’ constituents, have received a large backlog all at once.

Sharon from Hayle had waited a year for an operation when she received a call from the hospital asking whether she intended to attend. The appointment letter, together with the swabs required pre surgery, had never arrived. Thankfully, the arrangements were later confirmed by phone and email, but the letter itself was delivered three days after the operation had taken place. Another constituent was sent a letter for a hospital appointment 19 days after it was scheduled. Such delays risk causing vulnerable people to miss essential treatment, and place a burden on our overstretched NHS.

In Cornwall, our remote coastal geography and patchy digital connectivity—to say the least—mean that many of us still rely heavily on the universal postal service, but I worry that the situation will only get worse. In recent weeks, several Royal Mail workers have contacted me with concerns about the new delivery model 26. They report unmanageable workloads, experienced workers leaving, morale at rock bottom and substantial volumes of mail sitting undelivered. Three workers completing four rounds does not sound a credible way to improve reliability and restore public trust in Royal Mail. I echo the points made: the issue is not one of posties; it is one of management. Nor should Royal Mail continue to respond, if at all, to our constituents with template responses or hide behind impossible-to-navigate AI chatbots, while the reality on the ground slips further behind.

I therefore ask the Minister what discussions the Government have had with Royal Mail about DM26, and what action will be taken to ensure my constituents receive a postal service worthy of the word “royal”. If Royal Mail is going to treat this House and elected Members with such arrogance, the Government must take direct, firm and urgent action.

speaker: Lord Nagaraju
heading: Procedural Flexibility: Scrutiny of AI and Emerging Technology - Question
text: My Lords, I beg leave to ask the Question standing in my name on the Order Paper. In doing so, I draw attention to my AI and digital interests set out in the register.

speaker: Lord Ponsonby of Shulbrede
