speaker: Lord Holmes of Richmond
heading: Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill - Report
text:
My Lords, I apologise for not getting to my feet before our Front Bench. I was clearly so moved by the eloquence and erudition of the noble Lord, Lord Clement-Jones, that it slowed my motor function, and by the speed of my noble friend Lord Camrose, who clearly has his Asics on today. I very much support Amendment 61. There is so much talk about AI sovereignty, data sovereignty and digital sovereignty with it potentially meaning different things to each speaker of the sovereignty spiel. We need greater clarity across this. In the Bill before us, having this comprehensive clause covering what is required when it comes to digital sovereignty for the United Kingdom makes complete sense.

Moving to the Computer Misuse Act, the noble Lord, Lord Clement-Jones, my noble friend Lord Arbuthnot, I and others have pushed various Governments over at least a decade on this issue. Our cyber professionals, those who do so much to keep us safe, often and understandably in silence and in the shadows, deserve our support. It cannot be that they are still on the wrong side of a statute that is racing towards its 40th birthday. We should update the Computer Misuse Act. The noble Lord, Lord Clement-Jones, has offered a pragmatic solution in his proposed new clause, with a 12-month period to bring this to fruition. Our cyber professionals do so much; they deserve our support. This proportionate amendment should be accepted by the Government and put in the Bill.

speaker: Ali France
heading: BILLS
subheading: Online Safety Amendment (Digital Duty of Care) Bill 2026; Second Reading
text:
Continuing on from earlier, these laws are about protecting people from harm. They're about setting basic standards and giving social media users more choice over what they see. It will require big tech to provide a safe online environment, in particular for our kids. Our country needs this; our kids need this.

This month, the AFP has told us about and spoken of online child exploitation and victimisation, like on nudify apps. They've also spoken about online abuse and accounts; the manosphere; images and videos that glorify violence, porn and misogyny; and content that encourages eating disorders. Suicide is having a devastating impact, and all of this content is having a devastating impact on our kids. It has real-world consequences.

I spoke earlier about the number of comments that I receive on my social media accounts. If you had a side look at my socials for a minute, you'd see that, over the last 18 months, I've had tens of thousands of comments threatening my personal safety, calling me 'peg leg', calling me 'NDIS scum' and telling me that they hope my other son dies. Last week, one person wrote:

know where your family lives, run or burn

which was reported to the AFP. In the week before, Adrian said:

you are a delusional—

bleep—

retard that needs a hot poker shove up your—

bleep. John said:

jump off a building already—

bleep bleep. Jamie said:

I prefer assassinations.

Leroy said:

Someone shoot this dopey—

bleep. And, on the day after Helen's attack, Josh said:

are you gonna get the AFP to knock on my door for 'intimidating you'

We know that words and other content online and in the media fuel violence, threats and abuse in real life, not just for MPs but for teachers, health workers and retail workers. The Minister for Social Services, Tanya Plibersek, said yesterday that the explosion in social media tracks the explosion of sexual violence and strangulation. It's frightening. Kids, vulnerable people and people with mental health issues read those comments. They see and they feel the hate. They follow and are fed destructive content. There are millions of social media accounts that promote and normalise violence, misogyny, extremism and dangerous behaviours—porn.

We must demand better from big tech and the online environment. That is at the core of this legislation. If you run an online service in this country, you have a duty to keep the people using it safe. If you build it and put it online, you are responsible for the risks to users. And it's not just about social media; the games, the apps and the AI chatbots are all covered by this bill, as are nudify apps, which we heard today over 200,000 people have downloaded in Australia. That's scary.

We know what algorithms feed our young people: content that promotes eating disorders; content that glorifies dangerous behaviour, violence and suicide; and content promoting misogyny and the abuse of women. This content is seeping out of the screen and into our schools, our homes and our relationships. These are accounts that are, overwhelmingly, set up to menace and harass. Teachers are telling us about it. Young female teachers are now copping abuse in the classroom. They are telling us about attitudes that walk through the school gate straight off a phone or an iPad. It is content that radicalises, pushing young people towards extremism and violence.

This bill creates a single, overarching obligation—a digital duty of care. It requires the providers of online services to take reasonable, practicable steps to keep the people who use them safe. A duty of care is not a new idea; it is one of the oldest ideas in our legal system. We already ask an employer to take reasonable steps to keep their workers safe. We ask the builder to make safe homes and the manufacturer to make safe products. All this bill does is apply the same well-settled principle to online services that are now as much a part of our daily life as any workplace or public square The standard is not perfection. The standard is what is reasonably practicable—reasonable steps matched to the risk. That is a deliberate choice, because for too long the approach to online safety in this country has been to just politely ask the platforms, 'Do better,' with a set of basic online safety expectations and industry codes. They were a start. But, as we all know, that approach has been a big fat fail.

This bill replaces that with one clear, enforceable duty, set by this parliament, that every provider must meet. For young people, this bill goes further still. Providers must take particular care to protect Australians under 18 from the harmful material they promote. Where a platform breaches that duty of care it will face penalties of up to $109 million, enforced by the independent eSafety Commissioner. The bill also gives the eSafety Commissioner strong tools to act on the harms that are hurting Australians right now. It sets minimum standards for how complaints and disputes are handled so that, when an Australian reports something, they get a proper process and a real response, not a bot and a dead end.

This builds on the work the Albanese Labor government has already done to make Australians safer online with the social media minimum age and our crackdown on nudify apps and undetectable tracking tools that are used to stalk and control women. Then there is the part of the bill that hands Aussies back some direct control. We call it My Feed, My Way. Under the bill, social media services will have to notify their users—new users and existing users alike—and offer them a real choice over what drives their main feed, an opportunity to shut out the garbage, to switch it off. You can absolutely keep the algorithm and swallow that garbage if you want to, but if you don't want to you can choose not to: your feed, your choice. This bill gives you the power to make it social again, to make it about your friends, your family, your favourite charities and the businesses you want to follow.

Now, you would think that a law to protect Aussies from this would be a no-brainer, but we know that those opposite and One Nation will tell you this bill is censorship. They'll call it Big Brother. They will say that the government is coming for your freedom—which is just rubbish. Adults can still access what they want. The real freedom is in the ability to switch off the algorithm. We would not accept the harms caused online in other environments and other contexts. We demand that a car is safe before it is sold. We demand that a medication is tried and tested before it is put to the market. We demand that a toy is safe before a child can play with it. We should demand nothing less of the platforms Australians use every single day.

At the centre of this bill is one simple principle: that the best interests of Aussies should come first. On this side of the House we are choosing the wellbeing of the people who use these platforms over the profits of the companies that run them. Anyone who votes against this bill is choosing something else. They are choosing profit. They are choosing outrage. They are choosing harm. I know which side I'm on, and I commend this bill to the House.

speaker: Renee Coffey
heading: BILLS
subheading: Online Safety Amendment (Digital Duty of Care) Bill 2026; Second Reading
text:
I'd like to begin by sharing the experience of a mother in my electorate of Griffith who contacted me many months ago about the devastating impact an AI companion chatbot has had on her family. Her experience is deeply confronting, and it demonstrates why we cannot leave the safety of Australian children in the hands of technology companies that have repeatedly failed to protect them.

This mother said:

I am writing to you first as a mother.

My eldest daughter was seriously harmed by an AI companion chatbot when she was 12 years old.

I am also a technology founder who builds privacy compliance infrastructure for regulated industries, so I come to this issue from both sides: as a parent living with its consequences, and as someone whose work is in regulatory compliance and who understands what is at stake in getting it right.

In December 2024, my eldest daughter, then 12, was harmed by an AI companion app called Talkie AI.

She was first introduced to an AI roleplay website around the middle of 2024, at school, on a friend's phone.

From there it escalated quickly, and the harm built over an extended period of conversations rather than a single exchange.

During those conversations an AI character told her she was worthless and made references to self-harm.

Reading the exchanges back afterwards, they had the clear hallmarks of grooming and gaslighting.

This is not a historical event that we have moved past.

My daughter is in regular therapy.

The experience affects her every day.

She recognises it as a problem and does not know how to stop returning to it, and what we are managing at home now has the characteristics of an addiction.

Minimising her access helps, but it does not undo the harm already done.

Despite building close to a best-case home environment, including a physical device lockbox, a router with DNS-level filtering, device-level controls, a browser-free phone, and more than 100 AI roleplay and companion domains blocked manually, my children can still reach these platforms.

My younger daughter has since also been exposed, this time at home, through her older sister.

The responsible-parent ceiling is not high enough.

Debate interrupted.

speaker: Tim Watts
heading: GRIEVANCE DEBATE
subheading: Australian Defence Force Parliamentary Program, Artificial Intelligence
text:
'Everyday people doing extraordinary things'—that's the way Commander Paul Hardman described the work of his outstanding crew on HMAS Choules, who generously hosted me recently as part of the Australian Defence Force Parliamentary Program. I couldn't agree more with him, and I was proud as an Australian to have the opportunity to see it up close in person.

The ADF Parliamentary Program allows members of this place to step into the shoes of the Australian servicemen and servicewomen who we ask so much of as a nation. It gives MPs a meaningful insight into the day-to-day operations of the ADF through practical, immersive experiences. We get the opportunity to experience their workplaces, share their daily routines and gain a much deeper understanding of their lives and the responsibilities that they carry on behalf of Australia every day. I've participated in the program four times now, and I've always walked away with a feeling of deep pride in being able to see Australians in the ADF executing what they have been trained to do in the field.

I also want to put on the record that, in the decade that I've participated in the program, I've personally observed the way that the culture of the ADF, like this parliament, has changed. I was proud to see the diversity of modern Australia reflected in the young service men and women that I saw on this program. Real progress has been made on this front, and I want to recognise it here in this place.

This year in the ADFPP, I joined the ADF personnel taking part in exercise Keris Woomera 2026. Exercise Keris Woomera is a major bilateral military exercise conducted between the Australian Defence Force and the Indonesian National Armed Forces, and it was established by this government in 2024. The name Keris Woomera tells a story. The kris is a traditional Indonesian dagger, the woomera a traditional Australian spear thrower. Together they symbolise two distinct traditions working together towards a common purpose. That symbolism is important because this exercise is about far more than military exercises. It's about trust. It's about understanding. It's about building the habits of cooperation that allow two neighbouring countries to work effectively together when it matters most. Around 1,000 ADF personnel and over 1,200 TNI members participated in the exercise and conducted complex training across maritime, land, air and cyber domains. It's a significant exercise and a key element of our broader Indo-Pacific Endeavour program. The exercise is designed to strengthen interoperability, enhance combined operational capabilities and further deepen defence cooperation between Australia and Indonesia.

As part of KW 2026, I bunkered down with the REM on HMAS Choules, embarked on amphibious vehicles to land on the east coast of Java near Banyuwangi, slept in barracks with an artillery unit and experienced the South-East Asian heat in uniform with protective gear.

KW 2026 was a significant exercise for multiple reasons. It was the first time Australia's High Mobility Artillery Rocket System, HIMARS, was deployed and fired overseas. KW 2026 was also the first time that RAAF No. 4 Squadron deployed aircraft into South-East Asia since the Second World War. It was also the first time that Australia conducted cyberintegration training with Indonesia.

Participating in exercise Keris Woomera gave me the opportunity to observe something that's increasingly important in Australia's security and prosperity: the partnership between Australia and Indonesia. Australia and Indonesia are good neighbours and close partners. We're bound by strategic trust, mutual respect and a shared interest in a peaceful, stable and prosperous region. Earlier this year, Prime Minister Albanese and President Prabowo signed the Australia-Indonesia Treaty on Common Security, the Jakarta treaty. That treaty reflects a close friendship, partnership and deep trust between Australia and Indonesia. At its core is a simple idea: to keep Australia and Australians secure, we have to anchor our security in our region. Exercises like Keris Woomera show what that looks like in practice. They deepen understanding between our people and help build the habits of partnership that contribute to peace, stability and security across the region.

What struck me most during the exercise was not the equipment, impressive though it was, nor the complexity of the planning. It was the people. The Australian Defence Force and TNI are building something that no agreement or exercise directive can create on its own: trust—trust that comes from training together, solving problems together, spending time together. I had the opportunity to speak to both ADF members and TNI personnel throughout the exercise, and again and again I heard the same thing: they genuinely enjoy working together as partners. They value the opportunity to learn from one another. They appreciate the different perspectives each side brings. They recognise that every exercise strengthens relationships that may one day prove critical when our countries are called on to work together.

I acknowledge and thank all those who made my participation in exercise Keris Woomera possible. I want to thank my in-country liaison officer—makasih pak. I thank Lieutenant Alec Fuller for sharing an early-morning picket with me in Java. I thank Colonel Mark Tutton, Commander Landing Force of the Australian Amphibious Force; Captain Christopher Doherty, RAN, Commander Australian Amphibious Task Group; Commander Paul Hardman, the commanding officer of the HMAS Choules; Bombardier Max Vaughan, who demonstrated how to make things go bang on Java; and all of the ADF personnel who hosted us throughout the exercise, including my cabinmate on the Choules, Lieutenant Elliot Mitchell. Thank you also, as always, to Lieutenant Colonel Andy Martin, who does the important work of preparing all Australian parliamentarians to participate in the program. And I want to recognise Lieutenant Colonel Brett Edmonds, who I hosted in my office as part of the ADF parliamentary exchange before his departure. You're a credit to the ADF. Thank you also to all the Australian service men and women for our country.

Deputy Prime Minister Marles recently said that artificial intelligence is 'as big a sovereignty inflection point as we've seen since the Second World War'. He's right. A commitment from a frontier AI lab to train their models here could be the foundation of a new Australian-based AI industry that powers our security and prosperity in the decades to come. Hosting the training of frontier AI models in Australia could greatly expand the range of choices available to Australia in the rapidly changing and uncertain world we are seeing emerging around us. But the terms of that investment matter. Done right, it could commit the labs to invest in Australian researchers, put compute in the hands of Australian universities and start-ups and deal Australia into a seat at the table where the rules on the regulations and safety of frontier AI get written.

If Australia hosted an internationally significant share of the world's training compute, our voice would carry further with the labs and with other governments. We'd be wired into the supply chain of an industry that will shape the coming decades. We'd make ourselves indispensable. None of this will just happen, though. The labs have choices about where they invest. They weigh energy, talent, law and politics, and other countries are courting them. Winning this investment will take what Australia used to do best: an approach of our own—one that shapes things in the Australian way.

The Prime Minister has stated that the work with his framework on Australian standards for AI is intended to do this. The Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence has backed it. A letter to the Prime Minister from the committee on 12 October, signed by the chair and the deputy chair, said that Australia should not merely be 'a consumer of AI technologies developed elsewhere, but a trusted, competitive and strategically capable partner of the global AI industry'. The letter asks that any deal with the labs reserve compute for national security and our universities. It asks that the Australian Signals Directorate be given early access to new models.

But the committee also heard that there's a real obstacle to being able to realise investment in frontier AI model training in Australia. In my first speech in this place, in 2013, I noted that Australian intellectual property law was throwing sand in the gears of digital innovation and limiting Australian productivity growth. American copyright law has built the most rewarding economy for content creators in world history. Home to the biggest film and music industries in the world, Hollywood and the Grammys, as well as a video game industry bigger than both of them put together, it's a great place to be a filmmaker, musician, writer or artist. But US copyright law also allows transformative uses of content—using existing work to create something completely different. This kind of transformative use is the foundation of digital innovation, and there may be no better example of this transformative use than generative AI.

Generative AI doesn't substitute or compete with the products that it learns from. It learns from them and creates something completely new. American courts have ruled on training for generative AI and so far have found it to be a fair use. Australian law has no similar legislative protection for transformative uses. As a result, the work of Australian artists, musicians and journalists is currently being used to train generative AI models in the United States—in the words of the committee's letter to the PM—'without adequate control or payment'. At the same time, it's also why no frontier AI labs are training models here.

The evidence before the committee is clear: the status quo doesn't work for anyone—not the creators, not the labs, not the Australian national interest—nor does it maximise our sovereignty. And that's what the committee's letter to the PM said. It asked the government to re-examine our copyright settings so that creators keep control and get paid to build a better outcome for Australia—one that, if we can reach it, will be a world-leading settlement. Last month, at the National Press Club, former prime minister Kevin Rudd warned that Australia could slide into becoming a second-rate country. Missing opportunities like this is what would make us one.

speaker: Libby Coker
heading: CONSTITUENCY STATEMENTS
subheading: Online Safety Amendment (Digital Duty of Care) Bill 2026
text:
No matter where I go across my electorate of Corangamite, people are coming up to me and voicing their serious concerns about online safety. Whether they be parents, teachers or small-business owners, people are united in their view that social media has become the Wild West, with few constraints, and that the tenor of online debate is harmful, particularly for young people. It's why the Albanese government created a minimum age to have a social media account, and, so far, more than five million underage accounts have been deactivated, removed or restricted. As a result, YouGov has reported a nine per cent drop in online bullying, and exposure to inappropriate and violent content has fallen by 18 per cent.

This is welcome progress, but we know there's more to do—and that work is happening right now, with the debate underway on a digital duty of care bill. This bill is all about creating safety standards for the digital services we all use. It will force platforms to protect Australian children from harmful content and will ensure parents have the tools they need to keep their family safe online. For the first time ever, tech companies will need to do annual risk assessments of the harms their services can cause to Australians. They'll need to put systems in place to prevent risky features from causing harm, and, if they don't, they'll face serious penalties of up to $109 million.

That's significant, but so too are the provisions designed to tackle doomscrolling. We know doomscrolling causes real harm to young people. Locals tell me this all the time. Teachers speak to me about how young people are increasingly seeing more and more misogynistic and inappropriate content online. We know it's impacting their relationships with peers and, at times, their mental health, which is just so heartbreaking and so concerning. It's why we're backing the My Feed, My Way approach as part of our bill. It'll give Australians a choice. They can either opt in to the algorithm, or choose to only see content from accounts they follow. Social media platforms make significant profit from using the information of its users, so it's only fair that they give Australians some choice and follow the same basic rules as every other industry.

The bill also puts a stop to nudify apps. That means we're giving the eSafety Commissioner take-down powers to remove platforms that allow for generation of deepfake AI-generated nude images.

In closing, the bill in the House responds to so many of the concerns I've been hearing right across my electorate. I call on the parliament to unite in support of the digital duty of care bill. It's good for children, teachers and parents, and it's good for all Australians. It's about time that social media platforms are no longer the Wild West.

speaker: Mr Tony Stephen Burke
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE
text:
Thank you to the member for Cunningham for raising this issue. The cyber threat landscape is always changing, but the fact that we are under attack is constant. The defence minister just referred to the Annual cyber threat report from the Signals Directorate, where we had 1,500 cyber security incidents last year, an increase of 20 per cent.

This is happening at the same time that artificial intelligence is being used by those who would want to do us harm. We need to remember that artificial intelligence is not creating vulnerabilities. What it's doing is finding vulnerabilities and finding them faster than they would otherwise be found. The gap between a vulnerability existing and it being exploited used to be about 2½ years. It's now 10 hours. Artificial intelligence is supercharging the pace at which these vulnerabilities are being found.

The vulnerabilities continue to exist in three key areas, all of which are being dealt with and addressed in horizon 2 of our cyber strategy. The first deals with legacy technology, and when we talk about legacy technology it's not necessarily old technology. There can be old technology that we don't call legacy because you can keep patching it and you can keep updating it. But any technology or edge device that's not capable of continuing to be updated is legacy and carries risk. The second is the issue of the human firewall. So many cyberattacks involve social engineering where somebody is tricked into opening the doors wide—sometimes an employee, sometimes an individual. The final vulnerability is links that can exist within an entire supply chain.

Just as those who want to do us harm are using artificial intelligence to find and exploit these vulnerabilities, we need the same capability to provide the protection. The change that people will start to see as businesses and government are using the best technology to find vulnerabilities as quickly as possible is that patching of software is going to have to happen and happen fast. We've got used to systems with a whole lot of the businesses that we interact with where you wait for Saturday night, and Saturday night between 2 am and 4 am is when the update occurs. We are going to start to see occasions where sites that we are used to having available for us constantly look like they're shut down for a time. Overwhelmingly, they won't be examples, by and large, of successful attacks. They will be examples of companies taking cyberdefences seriously. We need to use every single edge that is being used against us. Our entire world now—our electricity, our water and every household device—is capable of being connected, and we need to make sure that we have the defences Australians need.

speaker: Tania Lawrence
heading: BILLS
subheading: Defence Legislation Amendment (Accelerating Capability and Protecting Bases) Bill 2026; Second Reading
text:
I rise to support the Defence Legislation Amendment (Accelerating Capability and Protecting Bases) Bill 2026. The bill should be understood as part of something much larger. It is yet another positive step in the transformation of Australia's defence posture that has been underway since the Albanese Labor government took office.

We are spending more on defence, but the challenge before Australia is not simply to spend more on defence. It is to identify the capabilities our nation needs, acquire them faster, build and sustain more of them here at home, reduce sovereign risk, firm up supply chains, work effectively with our allies and trusted partners, and protect those capabilities, the people behind them and, importantly, the places from which they operate. That takes investment, and this government is providing it at a level unprecedented in living memory. But it also takes strategy, industry, skills, partnerships, accountability and, saliently, laws that are fit for the strategic environment in which the Australian Defence Force now operates.

The bill establishes a new defence capability framework to support capability development, testing, evaluation and preparedness, alongside a defence security zone framework to better protect defence personnel, the facilities, the information, the activities and the capabilities. Importantly, the bill also provides for independent oversight by the Inspector-General of the Australian Defence Force.

I've spoken in this House before about Australia facing the most challenging strategic circumstances since the Second World War. In fact, there are more conflicts right now than there ever have been since the Second World War. This is not a slogan. It is the starting point for serious defence policy—policy based on our own needs and interests and the development of a sovereign capability.

Since 2022, the Albanese government has been systematically answering some fundamental questions: What kind of Defence Force does Australia need? What capabilities must it possess? How rapidly must we acquire them? What must Australia do to build and sustain ourselves? And how do we make our Defence Force, our economy, our infrastructure and our communities more resilient? There is a clear chronology to what then followed.

In 2022, one of the first actions of the Albanese Labor government was to commission the Defence Strategic Review, led independently by former defence minister and former foreign minister Professor Stephen Smith and former Chief of the Defence Force, Sir Angus Houston. I know both of these men, and I know the seriousness and the expertise they bring to their work. That review was commissioned within the government's first 100 days. We did not begin with an arbitrary spending figure. We began by examining Australia's strategic circumstances, determining the force structure needed to respond to them, and then identifying the capabilities required to make that force credible.

The Defence Strategic Review was released in April 2023. It identified six priorities for immediate action: nuclear powered submarines, through AUKUS; longer range strike and Australian munitions manufacturing; strengthening our northern bases; growing and retaining the defence workforce; translating disruptive technologies into military capability more rapidly; and deepening Australia's diplomatic and defence relationships across the Indo-Pacific. As I've said previously in this House, thanks indeed to the extraordinary leadership of ministers Marles, Conroy, Keogh, Kahlil and Thistlethwaite, a great deal has followed on from that strategic review process.

In March 2023, Australia, the United States and the United Kingdom announced the AUKUS optimal pathway. That pathway provides for increasing submarine visits; the Submarine Rotational Force-West, from as early as next year; Australia's acquisition of Virginia class submarines, from the early 2030s; and, ultimately, the construction of SSN-AUKUS. For Western Australia, this is very real. HMAS Stirling will sit at the centre of the Submarine Rotational Force-West, with a planned rotational presence from as early as next year of one UK and up to four US conventionally armed and nuclear powered submarines. That means infrastructure, engineers, apprentices, nuclear stewardship, security, maintenance, sustainment and Australian supply chains. It means the development of sovereign Australian capability.

In April 2024, the government delivered Australia's first national defence strategy, establishing a strategy of denial as the cornerstone of defence planning and directing the ADF towards becoming an integrated, focused force. Modern deterrence requires integration across maritime, land, air space and cyber domains. It requires intelligence, resilient infrastructure and supply chains, advanced technology and a strong Australian industrial base, and that requires investment. The 2024 National Defence Strategy provided an additional $5.7 billion over four years and $50.3 billion over the decade above the previous Defence funding trajectory. The Australian Guided Weapons and Explosive Ordnance Plan committed $16 billion to $21 billion across the decade, including Australian manufacture of the Guided Multiple Launch Rocket System missiles and maintenance of the Naval Strike and Joint Strike missiles. Buying capability is one thing; being able to replenish it, repair it, modify it and sustain it in a crisis is another.

That same year, Labor also introduced legislation for a dedicated Parliamentary Joint Committee on Defence modelled in significant respects to the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security, on which I serve, and able to deal with the classified information. A statutory Defence committee had been a bipartisan recommendation actually over several parliamentary reports. When we build capability, we also have to build proper parliamentary oversight. The coalition, unfortunately though, played politics and failed to support the bill at that time and delayed the establishment of the committee.

In 2025, much of this planning became increasingly tangible. In January, the government committed another $262 million to develop Australia's AUKUS submarine supply chain, supporting around 125 Australian businesses with the skills, security, accreditation, manufacturing, equipment and qualifications for international submarine supply chains. Then, in September, the Prime Minister announced $12 billion in new funding for the Henderson defence precinct in Western Australia. By then the additional Defence investment over the decade had reached $70 billion.

Henderson will support continuous naval ship building, AUKUS, surface-vessel sustainment and future submarine support, with the government projecting more than 10,000 local jobs. On any visit there, you will see the place and how it's transforming. The energy, the absolute dedication and focus across all tiers of government—local, state and federal—is actually an extraordinary example of how we can work fast and collaboratively where it's needed on such a priority project.

The Prime Minister spoke of investment in both our capability and our relationships. That is an important distinction. Sovereign capability does not mean strategic isolation. Australian capability becomes stronger when Australian industry and workers are connected to the technology, the expertise and the scale of trusted partners. We are also seeing emerging technology move from theory to practice. During Exercise Talisman Sabre in July 2025, AUKUS partners deployed autonomous and remotely operated underwater vehicles and advanced algorithms aboard an Australian P-8 maritime patrol aircraft. Later that year, more than 200 defence personnel, scientists and industry participants tested around 30 next-generation capabilities through Maritime Big Play.

In December, the government announced major reform of capability acquisition and sustainment, including the creation of a dedicated Defence Delivery Agency and Australia's first National Armaments Director. Labor also reinforced the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Defence legislation in October 2025, and it finally passed both houses on 4 March this year. So today Australia has a statutory Parliamentary Joint Committee on Defence with legislative scrutiny and parliamentary oversight, and that matters. The larger Defence becomes, the more sophisticated its capabilities become and the more tax money we obviously invest, so a stronger case is made for rigorous parliamentary oversight. Supporting Defence and scrutinising Defence are not competing objectives. Strong accountability makes Defence stronger.

Then we come to this year. The government has again increased the scale and pace of reform. The 2026 National defence strategy and Integrated Investment Program bring the combined additional investment to $117 billion over the decade to 2035-36. The 2026 strategy places greater emphasis on self-reliance, sovereign industrial resilience, international industrial partnerships, national civil preparedness and resilience. Under the NATO methodology, Defence spending is projected to reach three per cent of GDP by 2033. That is why the acquisition reforms matter.

The Defence Delivery Group commenced on 1 July 2026, with reforms intended to provide clearer accountability, stronger contestability and better cost estimation and assurance as Defence transitions towards the Defence Delivery Agency. The government's Rebuilding defence capability report says that with increased investment comes a clear responsibility to ensure Defence has the structures, the skills and the systems necessary to turn that strategy into real capability for the ADF. That task, of course, is made more urgent by the speed of technological change. Artificial intelligence, autonomous systems, quantum technology, hypersonics, long-range strike, undersea warfare and directed energy systems are developing extraordinarily quickly.

That brings us directly back to the bill. Modern military capability is increasingly developed with Australian companies, scientists, universities, researchers, engineers, startups, major primes and international partners. The new Defence Capability Framework provides a statutory foundation for developing, testing, evaluating and sustaining that capability. But speed must not come at the expense of safeguards, so the framework does not authorise military operations, intelligence collection or law enforcement activity, nor does it create a general exemption from Australian law or remove environmental heritage or native title protections.

The Defence Security Zone Framework addresses the other half of the equation: protecting what we build. Existing Defence security laws were written in years past, and Defence has identified gaps and inconsistencies, including in responding to contemporary threats such as drone incursions. It makes little sense to spend billions developing sophisticated military capabilities while leaving the people, the places and the technology supporting them vulnerable because our laws have not kept pace. The bill addresses that gap.

I just want to return to WA, because for Western Australia sovereign capability is already becoming real. Henderson and HMAS Stirling, as I said, are central to the story, but so are Western Australian businesses. I've spoken previously in this House about Hofmann Engineering in Ashfield and Bayswater, in my electorate of Hasluck, becoming the first qualified Australian company to receive a request for a quote to supply parts into the United States submarine supply chain. The Hofmann story demonstrates what sovereign capability can mean. A business that began as a backyard operation developed into an internationally connected Australian engineering company—Australian engineering, Australian workers and Australian skills connected into one of the most sophisticated defence industrial networks in the world. That is what AUKUS can look like in an Australian suburb, and that is why defence industry policy is a national security policy. Our security depends not just on what Australia can buy but on what we can build, what we can repair and what we can sustain and replenish.

Amid all of these strategies, investment programs, submarines, missiles and technologies, we should never lose sight of one thing: Defence is ultimately about people. Before coming to this place, I served in the signals reserves, and that experience gave me an enduring appreciation of the responsibilities that come with service and of the people who put on our nation's uniform. Since coming to parliament, I have continued to maintain that connection, including through Exercise Pitch Black, the ADF exchange programs and hosting officers from the ADF through the ADF parliamentary internship program. I'm also engaged through the ANU national security program, and I encourage every MP and senator in this place to participate in the same.

So this bill matters. Capability matters because we may ask our Australian service men and women to use it. I will conclude by saying that we are working now to develop that capability faster and to protect the capability better. I commend the bill to the House.

The right hon. Gentleman’s intervention was longer than my speech has been so far. When I find that I agree with every word that somebody is saying, I usually sit down and listen to a bit more of it rather than trying to challenge it. Perhaps the rest of my speech will answer the questions that he raises.

In that decade, because of the predictability and certainty of growth, I think that growth policy was seen like any other policy. In other words, if there was a shelf with all the different policies of Government on it, growth would be one set of policies on that shelf. I know that there are a lot of analogies going around these days, and Liz Truss has blown a hole in analogy use as well as in our economy, but it is my belief that we now need to have the mindset that growth is the shelf itself. We cannot have successful social policies delivered in the way that all of us in this Chamber would like unless we have a solid, predictably-growing economy into the long term that provides security and prosperity and from which we can share investment fairly around the country.

We must on both sides of the House be as animated about economic growth as we are about creating prosperity, spending it and challenging the social ills in our society. We must care as much about economic growth as we do about rough sleeping, social care and international development—I say that as someone who spent my early life in international development. Tackling those issues depends on economic growth itself.

Public services are incredibly important. They are enablers of growth. We cannot have growth if people are arriving late to work, are too sick to work or are stuck on a Tory waiting list for treatment. We need to have the right skills in the right places. All of those things are absolutely essential, but we should not kid ourselves that such growth is not built on by private enterprise.

Thanks to the Prime Minister deciding that I could have some time over the summer, I was able to write an essay—now that Tony Blair has brought them back into fashion. I know that many Members will have already read it, making some of my words today obsolete, but let me refresh their minds about what I focused on. I confined the essay to my experience in Government and how we can configure Government more assiduously and dependably to unlock the economic growth that our country needs so much—focusing on what Government themselves can deliver. That experience comes from leading two Departments as Secretary of State. I saw in both those Departments that civil servants can deliver boldly when they have the authority to and when incentives align.

I will use one example—the automotive sector—to illustrate to Members the challenges that the Government face to unlock growth. Delivering support for the automotive sector means aligning energy, trade, regulation and all these different areas of policy. All are held by more than one Government Department, and each of those Departments has its own priorities. As Secretary of State in the Department for Business and Trade, at times I was prioritising the automotive sector and recognising how important it can be for growth. Let us bear in mind, when Jaguar Land Rover suffered its cyber-attack, 0.2% was taken off our GDP. When it was up and running six weeks later, 0.2% was returned to our GDP. The importance of industry is still fundamental. When the Prime Minister and the Chancellor talk about reindustrialisation, hon. Members should not underestimate its ability to deliver growth for our overall economy.

We have another asset when it comes to the automotive sector in our country. When we talk about frontier technology—I am looking for the Minister for Artificial Intelligence, who was in his place a moment ago—we think about the AI labs, most of which are in California, with some in China, but we have a frontier industry here in the UK in the automotive sector, and it is Formula 1, because 11 of the 12 teams do all their research and development and all the deployment of their vehicles right here in the UK. No other country in the world has that asset, and that filters skills through our automotive sector. The ability to grow that sector is huge, but that needs Government to work in an aligned way.

I discovered how different Departments with different priorities have oversight over things like automotive, and how sometimes they can slow down those priority areas. We need the structures and incentives in Government to be much better aligned, because we cannot have all these important sectors depending on Ministers’ ability to WhatsApp each other to sort out problems. We should have a system of Government that is already on the side of making pro-growth choices.

I want to say a few brief words about defence, which has already been raised in the debate. I am grateful to the Chancellor for the statements he has made on this. We focus on the percentage of GDP allocated to defence, but the debate cannot just be about how big a share of our economy we spend on defence; it must also be about how big an economy we have. If we were to achieve five years of 3% annual growth, 3% of our national income on defence would deliver almost the same amount of money as moving to 3.5% in an economy of today’s size.

speaker: Tim Wilson
heading: BILLS
subheading: Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No. 4) Bill 2026; Consideration in Detail
text: Thank you, Speaker, for the consistency we're getting now in decision-making from the House, so that we can have free debate. I simply cannot understand: the member for Wentworth has laid the groundwork for higher taxes on her constituents and of course constituents in Kooyong, Curtin, Warringah, Wentworth and other seats, like Bradfield, and now they're trying to patchwork it and cover up the tracks of the higher taxes that are being imposed on small businesses, on innovative businesses, by making relatively minor amendments about structural problems. The issue and the challenge we face right now is that early-stage startups, innovative businesses—those most likely to contribute to economic growth, future jobs and employment, particularly in sectors like artificial intelligence, biotechnology and technology overall—have put their faith in the member for Wentworth. What has happened in practice is that the Treasurer has played her like a fiddle on these tax reform measures. As a consequence, all those businesses are now paying higher taxes.

speaker: Lord Leong
heading: Small and Medium-sized Enterprises: AI Sector - Question
text: My Lords, the Government’s core evidence is the AI sector study. The 2024 study found that SMEs make up 96% of UK AI firms, and nearly 90% of firms surveyed expected revenue growth within a year. To encourage investment, the sovereign AI fund, backed by up to £500 million, invests directly in British AI start-ups, alongside free compute through the AI research resource, Innovate UK’s £130 million growth catalyst, and a £100 million R&D procurement scheme.

speaker: Lord Leong
heading: Small and Medium-sized Enterprises: AI Sector - Question
text: As Minister for Small Businesses, I spend every day talking to businesses of all sizes, including small AI start-ups. We must ensure that small companies have access to finance to start their business. At the same time, we need to encourage young people to take up AI skills. We are committed to training 10 million young people in AI skills and, so far, 2.2 million have completed programmes.

speaker: Scott Arthur
subheading: Social Media: Ban for Under-16s — [Sir Roger Gale in the Chair]
text:
Like so many problems in the world, the solution can be found in Scotland. Young people in Scotland can use a Young Scot card to verify that they are 16, but I understand my hon. Friend’s point.

It is critical that, alongside robust age-assurance measures, online platforms be required to be as safe as possible for all users, both young people and adults. A ban cannot be used as an excuse by companies not to comply with their responsibilities, and important questions remain about the scope of the ban and the regulation of high-risk features. In July, I welcomed the Government’s further commitment to require infinite scrolling features to be switched off by default. However, there is more work to be done on location-sharing features for under-16s, as well as further regulation of AI chatbots.

I accept and understand the point that for some people, such as those who are struggling with mental health problems, health problems or perhaps their sexuality, going to social media may be a source of really good information. However, I am also concerned that young people who go to social media for advice on those really sensitive issues might end up interacting with people whose motivations are not good, and I think we have to be very mindful of that.

speaker: Zarah Sultana
heading: Petition - Coventry City Council contract with Palantir Technologies
text:
I rise to present a petition on behalf of residents of Coventry South regarding Coventry city council’s contract with Palantir. More than 3,900 people have signed a related online petition. In September 2025, Coventry city council awarded Palantir a contract worth £500,000 to provide AI-related services in children’s services. The contract was renewed in February 2026 at a cost of £750,000, a 50% increase, bringing the total to £1.25 million.

There are serious concerns about Palantir’s involvement in military and immigration operations, including providing surveillance infrastructure to the Israeli Government, which are committing genocide in Palestine, as well as the handling of sensitive personal data and the growing privatisation of our public services. The petitioners therefore request that the House of Commons urge the Government to call on Coventry city council to terminate its contract with Palantir, to consult residents and trade unions and to ensure transparency, accountability and democratic public control over the use of data in our public services.

Following is the full text of the petition:

[The petition of residents of the constituency Coventry South,

Declares that Coventry City Council has renewed a £750,000 contract with the US firm Palantir for children’s services; further declares that there are serious concerns about Palantir’s involvement in military and immigration operations, including its provision of data surveillance infrastructure to the Israeli government, which is committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, the handling of sensitive personal data, and the increasing role of private technology companies in public services; and further declares that Coventry residents, council staff and recognised trade unions should have a meaningful say in decisions concerning the use of AI and data in local public services before a contract is agreed and renewed.

The petitioners therefore request that the House of Commons urge the Government to call on Coventry City Council to terminate its contract with Palantir; consult residents and recognised trade unions on future AI and data decisions; and ensure transparency, accountability and democratic public control over the use of data in Coventry’s public services.

And the petitioners remain, etc.]

[P003257]

speaker: Lord Mann
heading: House of Lords: Relevance - Question
text: We know what we are, but we know not what we may be. AI will usurp the revising Chamber; that much is obvious. Is our future to be merely the hallucinators? The hereditaries flew their perch with barely a murmur, but what of us? Will we waltz into oblivion or quickstep into a brave new world?

speaker: Mike Martin
heading: Financial Services and Markets Bill [Lords]
text:
We on the Liberal Democrat Benches broadly support the Bill. Modernising a framework that has grown complex over decades is sensible and there is much here to welcome, from wider credit union membership to protecting in-person banking and tougher defences against financial crime.

I want to use my brief time to talk about a missed opportunity, and I hope the Government will take me up on it. It relates to the Chancellor’s former job. The Government rightly want to rebuild our defence industry, and small firms are one of the bedrocks of that goal. With the way that warfare is accelerating, the cutting, bleeding edge is with small tech firms innovating in things such as AI and autonomy. The Ministry of Defence works with around 12,000 small and medium-sized enterprises through its supply chains, and spends about £5 billion a year with them. It is further set out in the defence investment plan and the strategic defence review that the MOD wants to spend a further £2.5 billion with SMEs by the summer of 2028. That is where defence is moving—if we want to win wars in the modern age, we have to have a robust defence SME sector,

Every small business, no matter what sector it is in, knows how hard it can be to raise finance, but many defence firms face an extra barrier. They are often refused bank accounts, loans or insurance simply because they work in the defence sector. SC Group—formerly Supacat—has won MOD contracts worth tens of millions of pounds, yet it has struggled to get investment or loans because it is not seen as acceptable. Another example is 4GD, which uses AI and robotics to run training simulators for British soldiers; the company stopped attending investment meetings and was actually turned away from one once the host found out it was a defence firm.

A couple of years ago, 15 SME defence firms formally raised the issue with their trade body, ADS, as they had actually had accounts closed by UK financial institutions. Obviously, those were just the firms that were willing to speak up; there are plenty that will have suffered adverse reactions when seeking credit but have chosen not to speak out—because what firm wants to advertise that they are unable to get capital or credit? The crucial point is that this is not because of regulation. In March 2025, the FCA stated very plainly that:

“There is nothing in our rules, including those related to sustainability, that prevents investment or finance for defence companies.”

The problem is that many investment and financial services firms have environmental, social and governance policies that explicitly name defence firms as being unacceptable for investment. The Government know that, because in the MOD’s SME action plan, which was published in July, they commit to working with everyone, from venture capital to high street banks, to make it easier for the financial sector to back defence SMEs. But there is a difference between knowing about a problem and setting out a robust way of fixing it, and that is what I want to focus on.

The Bill started in the House of Lords, where my noble Friend Baroness Kramer tabled amendment 67, which proposed a practical step that might go some way towards solving the problem. The amendment essentially required the Financial Conduct Authority to review how easily SMEs in sectors critical to our national security can get finance. More specifically, that review would examine the availability and cost of finance for defence firms, whether the FCA’s rules create barriers, whether lenders’ ESG policies, sector exclusions or risk assessments are shutting defence firms out, and whether defence SMEs find it materially harder to get finance than firms in other industries. Crucially, the review would finish with the changes that should be made to improve access to finance for defence SMEs—it should speak to the problems identified in the review.

When my noble Friend Baroness Kramer presented the amendment, among a package of others, the Government declined, saying that the framework was already proportionate to SMEs. I think something has been lost in translation there. Proportionality is not the issue; the FCA has told us that its rules are not the barrier. The question is about what regulated investment firms are actually doing. At the moment, nobody is monitoring that, but amendment 67 sought to do so, by mandating the FCA to carry out a review on a regular basis—once every two or three years.

I urge the Government and the Economic Secretary to use the Bill to honour the commitment made by other parts of Government to support SMEs—including defence SMEs—to have access to finance on a level playing field with other sectors. This is not a party political issue: in March 2025, more than 100 Labour MPs and peers wrote to banks and investors about exactly this problem, and it has also been raised on the Conservative Benches. On Report, pursuant to any conversations that the Minister might like to have with me, I intend to re-table the same amendment and seek cross-party support. I am pretty sure there will be robust support across the House. I would welcome the chance to meet with the Minister to discuss the issue, because I think we have an opportunity to strengthen the Bill as it goes forward.

speaker: Gareth Davies
heading: Financial Services and Markets Bill [Lords]
text:
It is a great pleasure to close this debate on behalf of the official Opposition, and to follow on from my very good friend, the shadow Economic Secretary—my hon. Friend the Member for Wyre Forest (Mark Garnier)—who has done excellent work both in this Chamber and behind the scenes to engage extensively with the industry. Indeed, I am sure there is not a lunch table in the City of London that has not been graced by my hon. Friend—all, of course, in the service of his great country.

I draw the House’s attention to my entry in the Register of Members’ Financial Interests, particularly my long career in asset management, my active involvement in the industry going back many years, and my current chairmanship of the APPG for blockchain, which is relevant to this Bill.

It has been a privilege to be joined by many Members from across the House who clearly have extensive industry experience. I firmly believe, as I have for a long time, that we need more people in Parliament who have worked specifically in this sector, and who understand its importance and its power to help and influence our economy and our communities.

I thank all Members from across the House for their contributions to the debate, but I will name a few in particular. The Chairman of the Treasury Committee, the hon. Member for Hackney South and Shoreditch (Dame Meg Hillier) who is not currently in her place, provided a typically detailed and very thoughtful contribution. She expressed concerns about whether the pendulum is swinging away from consumer protection, as well as outlining her concerns about the reforms to the FOS. I do not agree necessarily with everything she said, but the House is better for the scrutiny that she and her Committee provide.

Let me pay tribute to our country’s longest-serving Economic Secretary, my right hon. Friend the Member for Salisbury (John Glen), who moved with grace from museums to MiFID back in the day. He spoke about his mixed views of the FOS. He acknowledged that it is—in his words—an unreliable path to resolution, and helpfully warned us that we need to consider the challenges posed by AI to the financial services sector.

I congratulate the hon. Member for Peterborough (Andrew Pakes) on his appointment as the Government’s co-operatives and mutuals champion. I have to say it is an appointment that passed me by, but I very much welcome it. One person who has always been a champion of co-operatives and mutuals is, of course, the hon. Member for Harrow West (Gareth Thomas), who spoke of the high cost and burden of credit, especially for those in poverty.

We on the Conservative side of the House want sensible deregulation. We want less bureaucracy in our system. We want lower burdens and more growth. Where the Bill does that, we will welcome it and we will help make it happen. The Chancellor was right in his opening remarks when he said that it is important to recognise the cross-party work that has gone on already with the Bill. He rightly echoed the views of those us on the Conservative Benches when it was said in the other place that the Bill moves us all in the right direction. Having said that—I am loath to depart from the happy and collegiate atmosphere of the debate so far—I am reminded of what Disraeli once said:

“No Government can be long secure without a formidable Opposition.”

So, if Members will forgive me, I have a job to do tonight. In certain areas, as my hon. Friend the Member for Wyre Forest set out, we believe the Bill does not go far enough. I would like to highlight two areas in particular.

First, on digital assets, the United States has legislated for stablecoin. South Korea and even the European Union have their own regimes. Our competitors globally are moving ahead. That matters because stablecoins could revolutionise the way we pay for goods and services. Blockchain technologies could transform the way we interact with companies and the state. The Bill was our chance to set out a more advanced vision and policy agenda in those areas, but the Government chose not to.

Secondly, ringfencing forces our largest banks to separate retail banking from the rest of their business. That was right after the financial crisis, but the world has now moved on and our resolution regime has moved on with it, as my right hon. Friend the Member for Salisbury pointed out. If we look at our competitors from New York, Amsterdam, Frankfurt and Paris, not one imposes ringfencing like ours—not one. We believe that we should not either. The Bill gives a little and takes a little, but there is a simpler option. If true deregulation is the aim, we believe the Government should adopt the Conservatives’ plan to scrap ringfencing altogether.

No matter how well intentioned the measures in the Bill are—and I believe they are very well intended— I am afraid that I must point out that they are being brought in alongside a barrage of anti-growth taxation and regulatory burdens imposed on our financial services sector and British business more widely. This afternoon, the Chancellor praised Britain’s financial services sector, and I welcome his words; 13 days ago, he spoke similar words but then doubled the bank surcharge—a £1.5 billion hit to the very companies and people he says he supports.

It is all about choice. The Chancellor could have chosen to cut welfare, which is spiralling above £400 billion, but he chose the easier route for a Labour Chancellor, as my right hon. Friend the Member for Beverley and Holderness (Graham Stuart) said, and decided to tax one of our country’s most-important sectors. Be in no doubt that this will have an impact, and specifically, I fear it will lead to more bank branch closures on our high streets, which none of us in this House wants.

I have no doubt that the Economic Secretary will shortly reference banking hubs in her wind-up, speaking with pride about how the Government are rolling out more. She is right to welcome them—I welcome them too—but she should also be clear about who pays for them. Banking hubs are funded by the banks—every one of them. Cash Access UK is funded by the banks. The mobile libraries and the pop-ups in our communities are funded by the banks. We cannot celebrate banking hubs on a Tuesday and then the next day tax the companies that pay for them. I am in favour of banking hubs, but I would much rather the branches not be closed in the first place.

To her credit, the Economic Secretary understands the sector. She is respected in the City and she understands the importance of banks to our high streets, which makes it all the more disappointing for the sector that she did not act to prevent the latest tax raid. The high street bank tax is just one example, but we also have the hike to national insurance and higher taxes on carried interest. That all results in more jobs put at risk, more high street banks closing and investment and innovation heading elsewhere rather than contributing to growth here in Britain.

For the most part, the Conservatives of course welcome the Bill, and we have been clear about that. Sadly, however, it will do little to overcome the barriers and burdens that this Government have inflicted on the financial services sector over the past two years. Warm words cannot undo cold taxes. The world’s capital has a choice about where it goes, and the Government have not acted in our favour. The Chancellor has a choice: he can back the sector or tax it until it becomes uncompetitive, but he simply cannot do both.

speaker: Baroness Smith of Malvern
heading: Mobile Phones in Schools - Statement
text:
I thank the noble Baroness for the work that she has been engaged in, alongside our officials, in the scope of the certification scheme. That has been welcomed. On the point about whether the focus is only on safety, I think we have a broad conception of safety in the standards against which the certification will be made.

For example, as I said, this will be certification against the standards, including our world-leading generative AI standards, which recognises that cognitive development of children is an important aspect to be considered when thinking in broad terms about safety. I do not think that the certification will have quite the narrow scope that the noble Baroness suggests, but I reiterate the point that we are interested not only in certification of products but in research on what is effective, how and where, and for whom—we are investing money in that—and we are looking forward for other uses of AI in education, where we will produce further guidance.

speaker: Adam Dance
text:
Sorry—I totally agree with the hon. Member. It is really good to have cross-party support. Just as the Prime Minister has argued that we need mayors as a force to drive change in local authorities’ areas, we need one person in Government to drive positive change on neurodiversity policy.

You are probably thinking, “Adam, that is all great, but how are you actually going to do it?” To put it simply, I am asking the Government to do three things: first, to make way for a new Minister by restructuring current posts or amending the Ministers of the Crown Act 1975 to expand the number of Ministers we can have; secondly, to give the new Minister funded statutory powers, by presenting Parliament with a cross-departmental strategy for neurodiversity that the Minister would be responsible for implementing, because this does not work if the Minister does not have teeth; and thirdly, to appoint a Minister for neurodiversity, which is probably the most difficult and political part of the whole process.

That is obviously easier said than done, but, as with most things, the answer is there: it just requires political willpower. Look at the new Minister for Artificial Intelligence post in the Cabinet Office. We see this time and again with Government: we are told, “Oh, that is too complicated,” or, “Oh, that wouldn’t be practical,” but then the public kick up a fuss, and, suddenly, it is not too difficult and can actually be done rather quickly. Let us not forget that this is about 20% of the public.

Obviously, though, the Minister today cannot snap her fingers and promise to do this—I would love it if she could. That is just not how this works, and I get that. Instead, I ask the Minister to commit today to starting the process by having civil servants review cross-departmental policy on neurodiversity and the merits of a neurodiversity Minister, and then to meeting me and campaigners to talk through the findings with us and hear our suggestions in more detail.

I know that this proposal is ambitious, but it is the lack of ambition on neurodiversity policy that has got us into this mess in the first place. It is only with bold action that we are going to make a difference, because I do not want to live in a country where the next generation of neurodiverse kids feel as I did when they tried to shut my youth club, and where decision makers just do not get it and just do not care. I thank everybody for listening.

speaker: Ian Murray
heading: Digital, Culture, Media and Sport
text: The Government are actively looking at this issue, because we know from experience—we always use the Southport example—that when there are incidents or crisis moments across the country, people turn to their local news outlets and the BBC to find the truth because they are sceptical of what they are reading. In the meantime, anyone who is reading these AI summaries online should double-check with their local newspapers and the sources they are given to ensure that that information is true. What happens, of course, is the old adage: a lie is halfway around the world before the truth has got its boots on. That happens much faster now with social media. I am delighted that my hon. Friend has broken his habit in the House by at least mentioning Harlow in his question.

speaker: Adam Thompson
heading: Nolan Principles
text:
I will be as brief as possible. I thank the hon. Member for Mid Dunbartonshire (Susan Murray) for bringing the debate forward—we are all very grateful.

Despite what the media might have us think sometimes, I think people in my constituency are not actually that interested in the to-ing and fro-ing of us here in Westminster. Instead, what they want to see is honesty and accountability in their politicians and their Government. They want some breathing space from the pressures of the cost of the living crisis, and they expect that those elected to serve them are focused on the issues that matter to them most. When I speak to people across Erewash, they rarely ask about the sparring that has happened that week in Prime Minister’s questions. What they actually want to ask me about is whether they can get a GP appointment, if their train will turn up on time, or how they will make ends meet at the end of the month.

People need to know that politics is working for them. When confidence in politics falls, so does our ability to tackle the challenges facing the country and improve people’s lives. That is why the Nolan principles matter. They are about restoring trust at a time when many people have lost faith that politics can deliver for them. Rebuilding that confidence requires those in public life to uphold the highest standards of honesty, integrity and accountability. The Nolan principles are not about party politics; they are the core of good public service, and they help to ensure that decisions are taken in the public interest. They set out the standards that British people have a right to expect from those who are elected to serve them.

In the era of social media, where misinformation can spread quickly and public confidence is easily eroded, standards of conduct are more important than ever. People hear a lot about politics, but they do not always see reasons to trust it. The rise of artificial intelligence of course has merit. However, it has created room for the rapid spread of disordered information and misinformation. With political deepfakes—often from accounts registered from abroad—seamlessly depicting Members of this House doing or saying things they have not done, it is unsurprising that people feel distrust towards politicians.

I remember the incident last year involving the hon. Member for Mid Norfolk (George Freeman)—I have notified him that I would be mentioning him today. A deepfake video was created in which the fake version of him announced his defection from the Conservative party to Reform, which, of course, the real hon. Member had not done. It was terrifying for all of us here, because of how close to reality the video was, despite it being totally fabricated. Fake news spreads six times faster than truthful content online, and 70% of people struggle to distinguish between real and fake news. Two thirds of Brits now see misinformation as the leading threat to our democracy, and with trust in politicians at an all-time low, that should concern us all. That is why it is essential that all politicians uphold the principles of openness, integrity and honesty. Where there is uncertainty in the information space, people should be able to look to public servants for clarity and not be met with falsehoods or ambiguity.

Every story of poor conduct makes it a little harder for people to believe that politics is working for them. Trust is hard to build, and easy to lose. Once it is lost, regaining it takes time. And it has been lost. Just four years ago, Liz Truss sent the currency crashing and interest rates soaring; six years ago, Boris Johnson broke his own lockdown rules to host parties in Downing Street; and this year, Reform UK has been investigated by the National Crime Agency for alleged dodgy dealings.

This morning on the Floor of the House I raised an incident with Derbyshire county council, which had placed engagement sanctions on our brilliant local democracy reporter, Eddie Bisknell. Although I understand that those sanctions are now lifted, I strongly agree with the Leader of the House’s comment that it sounded like they were running scared from basic scrutiny.

Public trust has been seriously undermined. It is up to us, as Members of Parliament and public servants, to adhere to the highest standard of professional and personal conduct. If we want the public to regain faith in politics and us, selflessness, integrity, objectivity, accountability, openness and honesty are the life foundations by which we must abide. Public trust should never be taken for granted; it must be earned and maintained. That is why the Nolan principles remain as important today as they have ever been.
